LAMES' LETTER.

idy DEAR Nximiz, This is a quiet time in the world of fashion, and novelties of any kind are few, so that there is but little to chronicle save what is being worn at the various popular holiday resorts. Here, it may be noted, quite a craze exists for gowns and blouses of heavy unbleached linen made very simply with tucked or stitched skirts, and pouched bodices with yokes of coarse linen lace. When made of hand- woven linen these apparently plain costumes are not so inexpensive as they appear at the first glance, but there are several cheaper machine-woven linens which are very nearly as effective, and the cost of the lace is not a serious matter. A narrow black glace or velvet belt is generally worn with an unbleached linen gown of the kind described, and not infrequently there is a throatlet to match. The yoke is generally lined with satin, or, if economy is an object, with mercerised lawn. Other linen gowns arc trimmed with Yak or Spanish lace, two varieties which are coming into vague again and will probably be largely used on wool and cloth dresses during the-coming autumn. With the much-favoured linen dresses, hats of very rough natural straw are worn more than any other kind. These are often trimmed with ban- danna silk or with spotted foulard, and in a great many cases the trimming matches a blouse which is made to wear with the linen skirt as a change from the material bodice. Hats of fine brown straw are also popular for holiday wear and are pretty when trimmed with twists of brown net and sprays of shaded pink roses, or, if intended for travelling, they look well adorned with bows of brown and white ribbon and brown quills. Shapes are still for the most part large and fiat and slightly raised on bandeaux; but the tricour hat is again fashionable, and promises to become more so during the autumn.

Hats for the seaside should have as little colour as possible about them, for sun and sea air com- bined have a most blanching effect. A suitable one is of burnt straw, the brim lined with draped chiffon applique with jetted sprays. Mark-hal Niel roses-. outline the brim,, and. a bow of black velvet uliderneath- rests on the hair. The short full neck ruffle is of black and white-spotted net, finished with velvet loops. Underneath is one of the short mantelets just resting•on the-shoulders, where it is bothered round the top with a chiffon ruching. The loose pleating which comes to just below the waist is of white cashmere, and makes a useful little garment to slip on over a. blouse for morning or evening wear. The hat is of coarse straw, with upturned curved brim caught back with three velvet bows in front, and trimmed with ahaded poppies. Another shirt-for morning wear is of stitched pale blue linen, bordered down the front and round the collar-with a narrow band of navy blue taffetas, fastened with small pink enamelled buttons. The hat is of stitched linen to match, canotier shape, trimmed with a dark blue and white spotted foulard bow.

Toques are skilfully combined ot colours that shoal into each ocher, green.and blue and tender mauve, in a fashion calculated to make the best of a pretty face. A burnt-straw hat is trimmed round with a white and red tartan ribbon, and furnished with huge wired loops of the same. The vivid colours look strange in the midst of our neutral tints, necessitated by-the general mourn- ing. Tartan gowns are also displayed for sale, tastefully made and welifmished.

A tasteful dress is in pinkish fawn cloth, trimmed with bands of bright Paisley-patterned velveteen in sage-greys, dull greens, and bright touches of amber, crimson, and turquoise, with here and there a, vivid net of almost metallia green:introduced,, resembling the colour of verdi- gris. So sparingry-are the bright colours intro- duced that they-convey no jarring crudity of tone, but are worked together in a subtle and telling harmony. These printed velveteens are of English manufacture, and the beauty of their designs show how far we have progressed in the art of cclonring.

Linen is the favourite material for seaside gowns this season, the coarse-grained linens, for choice, and they are trimmed with crochet point or guipures, or piped.andlablithbanda-of-piqu4, a multiplicity of buttons,being, • a necessary accom- paniment. div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

The prevailing bane of the Coronation dresses will be white, and historical records will to some extent, fur- nish the Court modistes with ideas for special designs. The Queen's desire that materials of British and Irish manufacture should be patroaised at the Coronation will no doubt be generally followed. This would only he what everyone would expect, but if society women 'were to maks it a rule to insist upon a preference for Btitisla materials, something might be core for our drooping it dustries in the manufacture of sitki,brocades ribbons, lacs, and dress fabrics. At the same time the competition between foreign and home made dress materials is a matter that also rests very largely with our manufacturers. No question of patriotism will prevent business houses, dressmakers, sr , the public generally from studying tneir own interests. The Queen's expressrd desire with regard to the Coronation dresses, will he sure to have its due effect, hut only a limited number of women can be pis sent.and the fact of' their wearing British made gowns, will not hays much effect upon Britbla trade as a whole It:would be diffetent,if say,in silks.which are always fashionable, in some toxin or other, our own manufacturers could supply the trade. It is however, not °rile patriotic support from the public that is wanted, but also greater silk and enterprise, in the manufacturing industries, if they are to successfully compte with :he foreign made dress stuffs, which undoubtedly figure very largely in our wardrobes. The Musician's Company have offered a prize for a new Coronation March. The Cernpany is one of the oldest guilds in the City of London, and the prize is fifty guineas, together with the freedom of the Com- pany, which will be bestowed upon the successful com- poser. Whether the new March will be Accepted, or whether, in that case, it can be played cn the great or- gan in Westminster Abbey, remains to be seen. It has been stated that the Abbey organ cannot be ' used at the Coronation for fear that the organist could afterwards claim the organ as a perquisite, just the same as everyoce else assisting at a Coronation, seems able to claim something or other, in recognition of their services. There must however be some way out of such a difficulty. In any case it 19 to be hoped that success will result from the inducements offered to British Corn- posers, and the musicians who have agreed to act as judges, are Sir Waiter Psrratt, Sr Frederick Bridge, and Sir H rbert Parry' The Crown Prince ot Pt 11961 a has made the most of hia stay over here, and at all the country houses he has visited, he has gained friends by his genial, affable manner. Unlike his father, the Emperor, be is rather inclined te be diffidest, and reserved. As one would suppose. his training has been chit fly in the military school, but, though he may be one day head of the German Army, the Crown Prince is naturally more of a a btudent, than a soldier. He speaks French and lEnglish fluently, and if he bad been born in a more ' humble sphere of hfe, he would probably have been a physician, or, like Lord Salisbury, would have devoted hi, i.isure hours to chemical research, and scientific

studies, Nu One will lcok with very sanguine feelings to the " League Poiret seasickness ' which has been initiated by Dr Madeuf of l'aris. It is the league which bas organized the Congreas at Oster d, together with an sxhibitieu of devices, and mewl for the prevention and treatment of seasickness, which has been opened under the patronage of the King of the Belgians. Amongst other exhibits is aa apparatus for training people to bear the movement of ships, but, if the result is a course of machme-made sickness, it would be jest as wed to wait ter the real thing, and make one job of it. Every sufferer wculd be glad if the Congress ceuld dis- cover any means ot preventing or even alleviatiag sea- sickness, but, at the same time, it would be as well to wait and see before expecting very much in this directicn. For chilly evenings, and for general autumn wear, there is nothing more convenient than a cape, or short cloak. The golf cape met with immediate approval, and now something cn the same principle has been devised, that will serve a double purpose. This is the reversible cape cf checked, or Vain cloth, lined with tartan. So contrived that whichever is the inner material for the time being, appears also here and there as a trimming on the right tide. Thrifty girls are building these cloaks with a lining of brocade, so that for evening wear the silt side can be turned outwards narrow ruching trimming the fronts, and edge, a derp ,! removable frill surrounding the throat. In these specimens all that is not brocade is face-cloth, cf some pretty dove shade, or one of the quieter ter/ans. I few seasons back a transparent gown invariably , showed a black, g-ey, cr white foundatior —reeved ! with one timid patch of colour. Now we have changed all that, and the majority of us most indeed be grate- ful for the charming and delicate mixtures of hues, at present available. French brocadee, and French taste generally, are responsible for the idea, but concerning , the origin of cur follies,we care little. .Sufilice it to say that pink, blue, heliotrope,green, clear vallow,and faint Dutch pink, are colours used two and three together with excellent effect. A dove's neck, or a pearly shell, would seem to be the original model of these blends,and by a subtle tcucb their range and changeableness is extended. For now not merely are the pale colours used, but vivid scarlets. astonishing greens, and mandarin orange, are pressed into service. They are rendered possible by a skillet veiling with white,cream, or smokee-peari chiffon, with which they are made up, and so these gaudy shades thus subdued, are reckoned among the most delicate tints available, and they rival and even surpass the plain colours, br their " shot " effect, and by the play of light and shade upon them A dedebttul mode of trimming dressing gowns and jackets, is with cretonne flowers. The material is not tar to seek, and the requisite sprays should be marked on the cretonne by tracing a deep ink or pencil line all round them. This boundary will show threue,h on the wren side of the stuff, where the space within it should !be well spread over with embroidery paste. rwg once I thoroughly dry, the patterns can be cut out " round all the cracks ana corners " with no fear or ravelling, and wed merely pasting or neatly stitching to the dress. ! One important feature of there cretcnne-trimmed robes, is the absence of visible stitching, and this is managed ' by stretching gauze, chiffon, or the lightest net over all details to which the scraps are added. This thin screen delicately veils the colours of the cretonne, and helps to keep it firmly in its place. Perhaps it is tbe bead chains that have brought bright balls into favour as ornaments. The little globes range in sizl from that of a pea to a school-hoy's marb'e, and ! are of glass, crystal, or other glittering ware. On : velvet and ribbon ends they take the place of ferrets and of eieteigetten These sieele bills are sometimes used as Putter's, and the more bar diome of them, incanted on a ring, dangle from chains and bracelets. The simplest of these balls are merely beads, pierced, and these are threaded upon velvet ribbon, the width, and pile securing taeoa, no stitches being necessary. _ _

100 YEARS HENCE. Lancash" grew - I century'

shire One Vast A own. Lancashire's population, so to speak, grew with mushroom-like rapidity during the wonderful cent I` w hich ended last December. According to the Sisk books the number of people who now inhabit the county is 4,406,787. That is more than half the popu- lation of England and Wales was in 1801. It is lust a few thousands below Ireland's present population end that of Scotland. Dwellers in the busy county of tee Red Rosa far outnumber those of any shire in the United Kingdom. But what will Lancashire be like in a hundred years or so, as regards density of populace, houses and work- Shops ? To some extent I leave the answer to the speculation of the reader, for this marvellous ccunty, with her wcrld-wide fame, seems yet to have endless resources to provide for a vaster population. By tree- ing the progress of the past century, however, we may ebtain some idea as to what will Le the condition of things when the twenty-first century is heralded from its multifarious institutions, With more and mere technical skill among the people, increased democratic' privileges, improved methods of business, lightning-like modes of travelling, and a thousand otter entrancing innovations—all of which appear Co be in the air—to Pxpedite life and trade, Lancashire may have been formed into one vast unbroken city, with some of the fields now lying between the rapidly-spreading towns serving the purpose .of city parks and open breathing spaces. Present signs of the times also indicate what en amt.zMg network of railways there will be,and what a mesh of tram lines running trom one end of the county to :he other.

div.head: EXAMINER, FRIDAY, AUGUST 30, 1901
div.p: THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, AUGUST 30, 1901
The Blackpool of the Future.

Then take a glance at the signs of the timeg on the ES& coast. In ten years B'ackpool has more than daubled herself. Those, too, who wlsh to walk the foreshore may read that in another hundud sears there will prabably be a leviathian promcna,le—illarninated by the Lord knows what !—stretchicg from Morecambe to Liverpool or thereabluts. Ws not at all improbable. Shortly 1 will present some facts to prove it. Population. - _

At the end of the 19th century Lancashire's popula- tion was seven times greater than at the beginning. Therefore, if she continuss to increase at the same rate, the population when the' present century gives up the ghost, will be over 28,000,000 ! Many reasons/ might be put forward to show that she will maintain this pro- portionate devclopment in spite of the fact that the birthrate is alarmingly decreasing. In the middle of the 18th century the population of Lancathire's towns, individually, was from 500 to about 4,000 persons. The striking iccreares commi•nced with the beginning of the factory system about 120 years ago. Since then every industrial centre has added from 1,000 to 1,500 son!s to its inhabitants every rear, almost without exception. Will this be kept up ? If ao,what must be the interest- ing result in 100 years, or 200 years ? Da not thrtik for a moment that this increase has been bmught about by mere fits and starts. It has been a steady growth, step by step. Take the Ceces- nisi population of the whole county from the beginnine of the 19th century as an example. In 1301, it was 672,731, or about 10,000 less than Liverpool alone at present. Afterwards the graeual rate of irc.ease was as followsi—Population in 1811 was 823,309, in 1821 1.052.859, in 1831 1,335,800, in 1841 1.667.054, in 1851 2,031,236, iR 1361 2,243,744, in 1371 2.819.495, in 1831 3,454,441, in 1891 3,926,760, in 1901 4,406,787. You will notice that there is very little varianco f rom one decade to another. Why should not this regularity of increase be sustained?

div.head: Network of Trams.
div.p: The Network of Trams.

When taking a bicycle ride through the county one is struck with the miles and miles of fields, in spite of the crowded populations associated with the nurnerouß ndustrial centres. But the cycle spin discloses several nteresting signs. Talcs a run, say, from Fleetwood to Lytham. There are tram lines the whole of the distanc• —about twenty miles* You will also have beard of sug- gestio:.s to bridge the Ribble and carry on a tramway to Scuthport. When clever engineers, backed by moneyed ' , men, get an idea into their ingenious heads, we may rightly expect to sea wonders worked. Experience has taught us that. So some day we shall have that tram ' line extended to Southpoit. Teen why not straight on to Liverpool ? Let th 3 next cycle ride be from Liverpool to Bolton or to Manchester. Electric tram lines are sow being construeted from Present to Old Swan, Liverpool. From Prescet they go in tho other direction to St. Helens and Haydock, and on towards Wigan. It has been proposed to lay them to Warrington, and we may put it down aA a sure thing that they. some fine eay, will be continued to Manchester. In the inland towns what is taking place ? We find tram lines bianching from the centre of the town into the suburbs in every direction. What must be the next step ? To extend these suburban termini till they meet, arid thus tie the towns together 1 by an amazing set work of lines. rhe House Question. .

The result of this as regards the erection of d welling- houses, factories, and workshops, is evident. Along the line of tramways blouses will pring up in quick succes- sion, till towns are again linked together by Yuman habitations. Examples of this may be sren to-day en any of the new tram routes. Of course, it is hard to say wlsit form of vehicular traffic will be in vogue in a hundred years from now. But we may rest assured that it will be eomething that will bring the centres of municipalities very near indeed to one another. It is manifest that residences—whether semi-etached or in streets—in the future will be erected at tut thee distanct s from town centres than is the case to-day, on account of the rapid means of transit, arid the desire for better hygienic conditions. Hence the spaces now existing between our towns wi'l be quickly filled up. To suggest that in a hundred )ears the whole of Lan- cashire may be studlvd with houses, shaps, collie, and warchousEs, may appear to be wild and foolish. But it must he remembered that all our densely peopled indu trial towns to-day cyst before the inventions of Uargreavee, Arkwriaht, and Crompton, merely quiet hamlets or villages nestling at the feet of green hills, or smiling on the flsral banks of limpid streams and un- polluted rivers. Lack to-day. Ride say from Stock- port (Cheshire) along East Lancashire to Blackburn,and 'You never get out ot the sight rf houses and factory chimnors. Take other railway jmrneys—foe exempla, from o:clham to Preston, from Liverpool to Rochdale.

div.head: City and the Suburb.
div.p: The City and the Suburb.

Two other conditions will cause people and houses to spread in the fields now left between the large towns. One is the housing problem. This, it is hoped, will bring about the abolition ot slums and insanitary dwell- ings, and drive the wo:kers outside the town. Another thing. As tawns continue to develop, their centres, like those of our (-Ties, will become mere localities ol offices,, warehouees, and tradesmen's establirhments. This again will mean that the people will have to go further afield to secure places of living. Then have you 'never noticed that ail new factories and other work- shops are invariably built away from the middle of the I towns ? These new places become surrounded at once Iby dwelling houses. Our green fields, shady lanes. beautiful trees, and charming floral gardens are con- stantly being cut up by the builder. When this he gone on for another hundred years, how much of nor delectable meadows arid pastures will be left ? Who ca a eay ? Now there are no indicati,ns that Lancashire will net keep up her decennial rate of iv crease. Tes increment for the pact decade is bigger than most other ten-year periods dining the 19th century, when Lancashire's greatness in wealth, workshops, houses, and population was created. Compare the figures for yourselves. The following are the rates of increase at the end of each ten years since 1891 :-1811. it ..as 153,578 ; 1821, it wag 226,550 ; 1831, it was 172.941 ; 1841, it was 331.254 ; 1851. ir ..aS 364,182 ; 18in, it was 217,5Cil ; 1871. it was 570.751 ; 1881. it was 6,34,946; 1691, it was 472.319 ; 1901, it was 480,027. Therefore, whichever way you loots—whether at past or at present signs—rho question, What will Lancashire to like in 100 years ? presses itself with more force and I interest upon us. Our coming municipalities have cer- tainly great problems before them. Our future town and city councils will have to be made up of more expert men, better men of ecienco or technical knowledge, in order to petf )rm their duties efficiently.

A GIRL OF THE PEOPLE BY MRS. C. N. WILLIAMSQN, Author of "The Barn Stormers," "Festal.,lVA Sport,* "Miss Nobody," "Her Royal TAP...o- nes'," "Lady Mary of the Dark House," avo.

div.head: CHAPTER XV.
div.p: CHAPTER XV.

Tlll MAN " "There! I've typed a thousand. words in an hour I" I announced. "Isn't that good for an amateur?" "Splendid!" said John Bourke. "Shall I ever be as good as your other secretary, who left you to be married?" I wistfully asked. "There never was a secretary like you," he replied. "Oh I But is that meant for praise or—other- wise ? " _ _ _
"It's meant to tell you that I wish I could keep you for my secretary always." "Perhaps you may. I'll grow old in your service."

He came closer and stood looking down at my finished work, yet not seeming to see it. I felt that there was something which he wished to say, and. that he was thinking of the right beginning; but ' just as he had opened his lips to speak there came a knock at the door. Mrs. Jennett entered with a telegram sent on for Mr. Bourke from the hotel where he was living. He read it and crushed the paper in his hand. "I must go at once," he said. . 'But I shall be back to-morrow morning about half-past ten with some more work for you to tackle, if you will." '
"What were you going to say before Mrs. Jennett came in?" I curiously inquired, as ha held out his hand for farewell.
He looked at me intently, in a characteristic way he had, that always quickened my blood a Little. "Do you really want to know?"

"Very much, or I Wouldn't have asked." "And I very much want to tell you. But it's something too important to be told in a hurry. If you were offended I should not have time now to try and make my case good." "Am I likely to be offended ? " "I can't tell. I hope not, more than I ever hoped anything." 'Dear me 1 And I must wait till to-morrowl" "I had meant not to speak of this matter until you were out of this house and in those rooms' of. your own to which you seem so eagerly looking forward. But I'm not a very patient mart, I'm afraid, where my own interests are at stake; and now that the subject has been broached—" "To-morrow, then!" I broke in. "At half- past ten. It's an appointment." "Yes," he said, slowly. "You shall hear what I have to say for,myself. ' All this time he had been holding my hand, and I had forgotten to draw it away, for the conversa- tion had been very absorbing. Now I remembered, and gently pulled ,away. my fingers. One more quick, strong pressure he gave them, and then, with an abrupt "Good-bye until to-morrow," he turned, and was gone without looking back." "What can it be that he wants to say to me?" I thought. "Something so important that he is anxious about it—something he hopes mayn't offend me ? " That speech was puzzling, for it seemed .that, if the mysterious "something" were the one thing I dared to hope it might just possibly be, there could be no idea of "offence." Still, the expres- sion of his face more than the spoken words, perhaps, gave me a hope that went thrilling through my veins. And when his tall, alert figure had passed out of sight 1 lifted the band that he had pressed and kissed it. Then, ashamed of what I had done, I hurried back to the typewriter, and began to work as if driven by a merciless task- master. .

For half-an-hour there was no sound in the room except the tapping of the keys, the sharp "ping" of the bell which warned me when I reached the end of a line, and the rustle of the paper as I changed the sheet. 1 had just found out that absent-mindedness had caused me to make some odd mistakes, when I heard a ringing at the front door; but this was nothing to me, and I did not pause until voices in the passage outside the study sent the blood flying to my face. "He's out, really, your ladyship," Mrs. Jennett was protesting, almost imploring. "He won't be back to-day, I do assure you." "I am sorry," followed silvery accents, which in the fraction of a,second carried me back to another world. "I will Write a note and leave it, if you will kindly let me go into the study, where I waited once before." I sprang up from the table where I had been typing, and my heart was thumping against my side. Unless Mrs. Jennett somehow prevented her, in a moment more Lady Fee Ringwood would be in the room. She would see me; what would she think? "What does it matter?" I said, angrily, to myself. "I'm Mr. 13ourke's secretary. I'd rather this hadn't happened, but—there's nothing to be ashamed of. Anyhow, it's too late now. I can't run away." There was only one door leading into the study, and my imagination pictured Lady No just outside. ' "Oh, your ladyship," Mrs. Jennett was saying, "you don't need to trouble about writing a note. I'll give Mr. Bourke any message you may like to leave." Her voice sounded troubled, and its note of distress added to my confusion. If she were so anxious to prevent Lady Fee Ringwood from seeing me, perhaps there were reasons stronger than I knew for concealment of my presence. My face grew burning hot, and my hands trembled. I looked round the room, but no hiding-place offered, even if I could have humiliated myself to seek one. Mrs. Jennett was the arbiter of my fate. If she failed to keep Lady Feo out of the study I must be brave and make the best of it. "I would really rather write, thank you. It is so trouble," said the visitor, every word coming distinctly to my ears. Then the handle of the door turned, and Lady Feco Ringwood swept silkenly into the room. I faced her, standing, my eyes unflinching, but my cheeks scarlet. She started, and her beautiful face went from white to red. For an awkward instant no one spoke. Then Mrs. Jennett, quivering in the back- ground, stepped into the breach. "Your ladyship, this is Miss Harland, Mr. Bourke's secretary." "Ah, indeed ? " said Lady Feo. "I believe I have met Miss Harland" (she spoke the name slowly and with emphasis) "before. Do you remember, Miss Harland?" "Yes, I remeinber you very well, Lady Feo," I answered, and though I tried only to keep my tone steady it sounded defiant. "It is interesting to meet you again—here." She turned to Mrs. Jennett with a smile, looking a very great lady, as indeed she was. "I will write my note, and perhaps, as Miss Harland is here, she will take charge of it, so I need not trouble you. I am in no hurry, and if she doesn't mind, I would like a little talk with her. We have, I think, some friends in common." "If you are not too busy, miss ?" the poor old woman said, anxiously, to me. Her eyes added: "Do forgive me. I did my best. I hope this won't vex you very much." I sent a glance to reassure her. My spirit was roused, and I did not wish the visitor to go without some explanation; though I had arranged no formula in my mind. "I am not too busy for a talk with Lady Fee Ringwood," I returned. Mrs. Jennett disappeared, closing the door. , "Will you sit down?" I said. "No I" Lady Fe° ejaculated, her voice utterly changed in an instant. "No, I can't sit down." Her tone was a challenge, and I looked up to meet it. Our eyes met, "It's true, then!" she exclaimed. "I would never have believed it." "What do you moan?" I asked, quickly. "Did you expect—were you told that I was here ?" "Not that," she declared. "Not so bad as that. I was told that—eotneone was here." "I don't understand you at all, Lady Foo," / said. "But, of course, it seems strange to you--" "Strange? It is incredible !" "Not, incredible really; it only appears so," I protested, hardly knowing whether I was supposed to be on the defensive cut not. "I daresay you must have heard that—that I had a very great affliction, and, afterwards, misfortunes." "Oh, I heard things, of course," she cried, with a kind of fierce impatience. "But nothing, nothing which led rao to expect. this." “yet you said a moment ago that yoit had beard—" "I was not thinking of you then; I was thinking of Mr. Bourke." I felt the blood which had burnt in my cheeks receding, to leave me pale. Still, I.was at a loss to fathom her emotion. She had been on friendly terms with my adopted mother and me. The last Limas I had seen her she had been dining with us

and some people Lady Cope had aseted to the Savoy Hotel the Sunday night before my banish- ment. ,Did her excitement now mean surprise at meeting me again, and concern at seeing me so fallen in the world as to be earning my living as a typewriter, or was there something deeper than this, something which I should regard as offensive ? I was only eighteen, and I did not feel sure of my ground. "Mr. Bourke has been very kind to me," I said. "I am trying to help him as well as I can." "Kind to you!" Lady Feo echoed, with a strange bitterness. "But what has he been to himself? " "To himself ?"

"For him this spells ruin. Yon talk of 'helping' I Is it possible you are so blind as not to see that you are dragging him down—down off the pedestal his genius has given him?" I stared at her in blank amazement, my lips apart. "Don't look at me like that I" she cried, a sudden flame of anger leaping to her dark eyes. "I never thought that you were wicked or a fool, Sheila Cope. Now I believe you are both. Wicked for him. A fool for yourself." "Lady No!" I exclaimed, indignantly. "Yon 4141 older than I am, but you must not speak to me tiSC shot."

She had been very pale under a faint 'fink tinge stf rouge which I had not suspected her of 'before, but now her cheeks blazed and hid the hard line of artificial colour. "Older than you I" she repeated, intolerantly. "Three or four years, perhaps. But after this thing that you have done you can no longer pose as a guileless child." "I have done nothing," I answered her, hotly. "Nothing, except to lose all my friends and all my money, and be obliged to work for my bread." "You look like a hard-working breadwinner, in that Liberty tea-gown!" she sneered.

Before any -answe; had come to me, she went on. "At least, I see by your face that you have the grace to be ashamed of yourself. Then there may -be some hope yet." "I have nothing to be ashamed of," I did find voice to say at last. "I think that you and I, Lady Feo Ringwood. must be playing at cross purposes. Did you come here to insult me ? " "I came to save John Bourke—if I could."

"To save him—from,what ? " "To speak frankly, from great danger of losing all the fruit of his ambition. His seat in Parliament; his chance of rising higher still, should the Liberal party come into power. For a moment, in the shock of hearing that the man I loved was in peril of such a disaster, I forgot myself and the part allotted to me in this etrange scene. "ph, he must not lose it!" I cried.
Lady Feo looked at me with a curious expression. "It rests with you," she said. "With me ? Impossible ! " .._ . _ .

"But it is true. Listen, and I will tell you how. Mr. Bourke has enemies, as all strong men must have. It has got about that—that—well, that a mysterious lady is living in his house. All sorts of stories are being told--" "They are lie.!" I broke in, furiously, under- standing her at last. "Wait—if you really care for him. Hear me to the end. lam his friend. I believe in him as I have never believed in any other man. I would do anything to save him from the storm that is gathering. If you have any real love for him in your heart, any womanly unselfishness born of love, you will do the only thing left for you to do for John Bourke. You will leave his house."

"It is not his house 1" I cried, desperately, scarcely able to speak for the sobbing breath that came pantingly with the wild beating of my heart. "It is Mrs. Jennett's house. He is not living here. He has been at an hotel ever since I came---" _

"Oh, what sophistry ! Even if I believed it, what good would such a story do him, when he came to defend himself from the accusations which will be brought against him? Sheila Cope, tell me, as woman to woman, do you love him ?" "He is my employer, my friend," I stammered, "not my lover. Never has tone word of—" "Answer my question!" "I will not answer. You hare no right to ask." "You have answered. But I say to you you do not love him or you would leave this house now— this hour."
"I was going away in a day or two," I said. "It is all arranged. My rooms are engaged. I have been ill, and--"

"I don't Mean that sort of going away. You might sw well stay here, for all the gobd you will do to Mte. Bourke by moving to rooms which he has taken for you—" • "Mrs. Jennett took them," I cut her short, obstinately, tears of shame and anger brimming over in my eyes. "Oh, nonsense! It's all one. Don't play the child with me."
I adjured her with passion, "I swear to you by all I hold most sacred that you cruelly wrong both me and the man you love I" She quivered, and stared at me sidewise, her eyes flashing. _ .

""How dal:e you say I love him!" "You have dared to say things to me such as no one else on earth would have uttered. Why should I not dare? And I do say it—though it is nothing to me." • '44' For a moment she looked at me in silence, her bosom rising and falling under its soft summer laces and the bunch of purple orchids pinned in her dress. "Well," she spoke at last, more softly, 4you are right. I confess it. • For it may prove the touch of nature that will make us two kin for this one hour. I plead to you—l don't command. Save him—as I would save him, were I in your place—no matter how costly the sacrifice. You tell me Ido you an injustice. Suppose I do. Yet would men of the world believe it—the men he has to deal with? Why, I came here in fear and trembling, praying I might do something. But I should have feared far more—always-for John Bourke's future—if I'd dreamt that the girl I had heard of in this house was Sheila Cope." "Again I don't understand," I said, miserably, my heart so cold that it seemed to freeze all flexibility from my voice. It sounded in my OWE ears like that of a very, very old woman. "Now that you are quieter and gentler,' I'll e4plain. Only, this time, you "must promise to hear me through to the end without interruption. Will you do that?" I nodded—for it was bard to speak.

div.head: CHAPTER XVI.
div.p: CHAPTER XVI.
A LETTER Olf TIIE TYPEWRITER.

"tverybody has been talking about Sheila, Cops and her affairs," Lady Feo went on, carefully, as if she were piling up her indictment, word by word, choosing each as a builder might choose a stone. "You have made conversation at teas and dinners, and doubtless in club-rooms; you have made paragraphs for papers. You began by being a popular debutante; you became a mystery; it remains to be seen how you will end. But don-'t speak yet. "It was known that, .by Lady Copes failure to make a will, or something of that sort—such stories are always vague—you were no longer an heiress. Roger Cope came into everything. He was in love with you, of course. ' We all thought that, those who 'knew him and those who didn't ; and he did not take the trouble .to contradict it. He, or someoue—it doesn't signify gave out that you had gone to France to live with relations. But you disappeared such a short time ago that people haven't yet lost interest. They are on the qui viva to hear the next development. NI hat Will be said of John Bourke when it comes out that instead of being in France you are in his house, calling your- self Miss Harland, and wearing lovely 'white satin tea-gowns ? " "I shall cause the truth to be said l" I pleaded rather than protested. "'h. would rather die than harm should come to him i through my fault, after all his goodness to me. I was penniless and almost • starving, Lady FiSo—so desperate that I was going to throw myself into the river, when he found me and brought me here, because I had nowhere else t0,g0..7

"All the worse for him, when the story is known. He will be called a scoundrel for taking shdrantage of your youth and helplessness." ' '4For giving me work—for leaving his home that sc might be a refuge for me when I was to ill to moved ?'; "That won't be what hi.s enerniee will say." "litnt-if I tell all—all, myself ? " "Nobody would believe you. 'Naturally a girl, taught in such a web, would make things lonic as well for herself as she could. It wouldn't help him—or you. Believe me, for I know tlie world. "What Ai-o'lld you have me do?" I den:ended. brokenly: "I have told you.. Go away." - / i "And I have said that Ilim going." "To rooms of 11-ivtaking.- Oh, Sheila, I beg of you, for his sake,' gb.-Tai away from him, and leave, no trace." . Now, indeed; I could control 'my tears no longer. They fell from my eyes like rain, , and sobs choked , \ my voice.

"Oh, 1 can't-1 can't do that! I ertu... without letting him know why or whet ' lie would believe me ungrateful—he wouLt telieve horrible things that are not tine." "If he did, you should be unselfish no ,h to be glad. For it would spare him pain. And it would keep him from searching for you, which he might do otherwise, out of a conviction that it was his duty to see that you were safe." "Perhaps you are lying to me!" I flung at her. "Perhaps you only want to get me out of the way."

Lady Ftio Ringwood smiled. "You don't really think that. lam not afraid of you with John Bourke, my poet ehild." I looked at her, and as my pain .and jealousy accentuated her_beaut7,l told myself bitterly that she had no need 'a SIIIVaid. She 'lvasft'lite •s young queen, in her exquisite dress and the black picture hat that contrasted with her auburn hair; ”daughter of the gods, divinely tall, and most divinely fair." I was a little insignificance; my poor claims to prettiness paling beside het classic perfection. "L saw," she continued, "from that old woman's reluctance to let me into the study that the Secret was there, and so I was determined • to entdr, for I I.ad come to the house with a purpose. I expected tab see some ordinary girl of no importance. I Nlund you. I said to myself: 'Sir Roger Cope will rflZZl Bourke for this,'or John will kill him; ' "

Roger Cope I "'I ejaculated. "Always Roger Cope!" "Yes, Roger Cope. But if he were the only one with whom Mr. Bourke will have to reckon it would not be so bad. lam so far from having lied to you that certain political opponents, who would give ten years of their lives to have him under their feet, have arranged to set spies upon him. Anyone who rings at the door-bell may be a spy. Or the servants will be questioned. Proof is what they want. It' is easy to get. Unless you go and hide yourself before it has been actually got. Are you brave enough? Do you love him enough for this?"

"I am grateful enough," I answered, haughtily. "Then do it—quickly, before you change your mind and weaken; quickly, before it is too late. If you do this I shall believe in you and speak well of you always. Some day Jack himself shall know." I shrank away from the gloved hand she laid on mine and shivered. I guessed the meaning cloaked by her words. She wished me to understand that some time in the future, when she was John Bourke's wife, and he was safe from all harm which I could do him, he should hear the truth about my going. Till then I must content Myself to remain under a cloud—a cloud blacker and colder to my soul than the river from which I had been saved by him. And she called him "Jack." "I will tell Mrs. Jennett that you have brought ille news which makes it necessary for me to go away," I said, as firmly as I could. "And—l will leave no message for—Mr. Bourke." "Ah, but that would be to defeat the end you seek to gain," Lady Feo assured we, hastily. "Mr. Bourke must not know that I have had any- thing to do with your going—for his own sake he must not, if he took the idea into his head that You bad been coerced in any way, he would certainly not stop to think of his own advantage, but would move heaven and earth till he had found you again, giving you back your position as his secretary— which perhaps you can ill afford to lose?" • "I shall contrive to get on without it," I replied. "You will let me help you, of course I It would be only fair, since by my advice you are giving up —your situation. "I shall not need your help, thank you," I said. For I would not have taken anything from her to save myself from starving. "I didn't mean you to go away without leaving word for Mr. Bourke," she went on, catching up the dropped thread with animation; for her offer of assistance had been but perfunctory and absent- minded. "It would be best to satisfy his tnind that you had gone because it was your own wish, because you thought that you could better yourself. Then, you see, his conscence would be at rest; he would be contented to let you alone; and the flame of scandal would presently die, let us hbpe, for lack of fuel."

"Very well, I daresay you are right," I rejoined. hopelessly/ "I will write such a letter.' Lady Feo's hand rose nervously to her breast, toying with the orchids pinned among her laces. "Sheila," she said, betraying slight confusion, "would you—you would not, I suppose, let me se* tiso letter when it is written, and—and advise

div.head: about it?"
div.p: about it?"

I saw that she meant to persist if I chewed signs of refusing her request, and I did not care to hold out against the suggestion. Since I was an-obstacle in John Bourke's path up the hill of fame,l wished to remove myself in the way that would be best for him. I was ready to believe that Lady No Ringwood knew what the best way was, not so much because I considered her a wise and con- scientious adviser, as because her revelations had forced me to certain deductions of my own.
John Bourke's words, which had made me so happy and hopeful only an hour or two ago, came back to me now, lurid in the light of a new meaning..

I sat down at the table from which I had risen at the sound of , Lady Feo's voice in the passage and deliberately placed a fresh sheet of paper in the typewriting machine. Then I bggan to tap out, letter by letter, my farewell to the man I loved. "Dear Mr. Bourke," I wrote. "It is easier to write some things than to speak them. After all, I don't think that the life of a typewriter would suit me. I have grown restless and want a change." (How my heart smote me as any fingers told the falsehood !) "Perhaps I was foolish to choose poverty when I might have had all I could possibly wish for. So now I have changed my mind. test you should not approve, and I should be forced to argue my point (I'm not good at argument), I will not ,wait to hear what you think of this step I am taking, but will say farewell now. Thank you again for all your kindness, which I shall never cease to appreciate. But I shall be happier in a life more like that to which I was brought up. In that • life we may not meet again; and so this is good-bye." Lady Feo's eyes followed each line as I typed it. "Well ?" I said at last, when I took the paper from tile machine to sign. . . . _

• "It is very well indeed," she pronounced. "You have given exactly the impression that it is best to convey. You couldn't do better." "I am glad you are satisfied," I said, in a stifled voice. I dipped a pen in an ink-pot standing near, then paused with it suspended. I had never signed the name which was really mine, "Jenny Harland," and to do so was repulsive. "I will not be Jenny," I said to myself; not to him at least. In this one "thing I will indulge my own wish. I shall sign myself " I wrote the name hurriedly beneath the few typed paragraphs, folded the letter, and put it into an envelope, which I addressed to "John. Bourke, Esq." I fel; as if I had signed ray oven death warrant; but'l wept no longer. A stony calmness Lad come to help me through the rest of this scene with Lady No Ringwood. "When will he be here again ?" she asked. "Not till to-morrow," I informed her. "Yon are sure ?"

"As sure as I can be of anything." "That's good. I will go now, for, as I said, I must not be associated with this plan of yours. Presently, I suppose, you cam make some excuse to that old woman—Mrs. Jennett, isn't it? You won't tell her that you are leaving for good?" "No—o," I said, slowly. "Perhaps it would be better. not. She has been very kind tome, and it is hateful to leave her so. But one hateful thing more or less doesn't matter much now." "Ikou are a brave girl, Sheila Cope," exclaimed Lady Foo.• "It sounds conventional to say that Heaven will reward your unselfishness, but, really, I believe it will." . _

"We Won't talk about it, if you please," I said, my lips very stiff as I formed the words. 'At all events you must come to me afterwards. Not to my house, perhaps, for that might lead to awkwardness—one never can tell. Things happen so queerly. But we must make an appointment. This is a est responsibility I've undertaken, an I fee!—" •

- "Don't feel," I cut her short, abruptly. "i shall be all right." "Have you—do forgive me—but have you atoney ?" Her hand fluttered towards a dainty, gold-netted pa rs e that she had laid with a lace film of hand- kerc,hief on Mr. Bourke's desk. I stopped her with a gesture. "I know where to get money, thank you." "Oh, very well. Of course you know your owit affairs best. What else is there for me to say?"

"Nothing but—good day," I returned, with & smile that was strained,aa the smile on a mask. "I have been very frank, very outspoken, because I had to be so. But I hope you don't feel hard towards me ? "

"I don!tihink that I—feel anything," I sal/ - "Well,tten, good-bye." I mum red something, and did not seem to see tips hand which she held out—a great lady con- descending to a misguided girl who had promised to mend her ways, and therefore deserved emu-

samadation. She gathered up her belongings and wend the door, then turned and looked at ma s* y. ~+Noit won't change your mind and—and still ri4gig all? I may—trust you?" eyes flashed to hers. ' "I am doing this, not for you but for All'• Bourke," I said. "I will not go back from Ls/ promise to myself." "Then I do trust you." She had the last word and so was gone. Mechanically I began to put away the material on which I had been at work. I had finished typing Mr. Bourke's article, which was to appear in the Fortnightly Review. Never would Ido aill more work for him. But he would find plenty of others. to atep into my place. I had only been employed out of charity. When I had neatly arranged the papers I had tio longer an excuse for inaction. I must make up re{ mind exactly what to do with myself. Somehow seemed always to be making up by mind what to do with myself; and as soon as the matter was settled Fate interfered to undo it all again. I had rull away from Arrish Mell Court; I had run awaY from Easel-street; now I was going to run aural ' from John Bourke, which meant leaving all that had become to me best worth living for. I had promised him that never &gain would I be a coward and seek to end my own life. I would not break the promise, and so my troublesome self had to be• provided for; plans made by which mi body was to be fed and clothed, just as if it were still of some importance. There was Roger Cope, of course. I could realll do the thing which in my letter to Mr. Bourke had hinted at. Probably Roger's offer was still open, and if I took it I could rehabilitate myself ill the eyes of the world, in case my acquaintance • with the great "Labour Member" became known to others beside Lady Feo Ringwood. Yet, no! I could not bring myself to that. I thought of Mr. Westerley. But he liked Roger, and would advise me to act in a way con- trary to my inclinations, if according to common sense. He was a dear old matchmaker, and with the best intentions in the world he would work t° throw Roger Cope and, me together. Therefore, , Mr. Westerley was still out of the question. My eyes fell upon a newspaper lying on the desk. It had not been there, I knew, before Lady Fee came. She had, doubtless, brought it in and for ' gotten to take it away. I picked it up and turned to the advertising pages. I could not go back to any of the agencies I had visited while I lived ill Easel-street, for Mr. Bourke was probably right • his deductions. At all events, they had offered m° no hope, after the first visits I paid them; but Roger had certainly lost sight of me now, and be could not prejudice the minds of advertisers in the papers in case I should luckily discover one willing to try my services. But I could find nothing in the long lists of persons wanted which offered hope for me, and I was on the point of flinging the paper aside with impatient sigh when my eyes happened to fall upon the 'personal " column on the first page. Then my heart gave a great bound and I snatchell up the paper again. (To be miaowed.) air'

with transitions and steps on the way—with pauses and new starts on the journey—and all these were cmditions nf advancement to progre-s If he tried to sum the thought with which be would leave the tr.son for which he had a growing affection. le must expre.s it in words of gratitude. Never could he b t thankful enough for thc kindness he had received during the past three years from all classes of people in the town. He had tried to share with the young men of the town in all their joys and pleasures, and take an active part in their difficulties, not as a parson,but as a man with a man and a brother with a brother. He lett them not knowing what changes yet awaited them. Be went out himself indeed not knowing what would await him,but this he knew—that no changes, not even death itself, need sena rite them from GncLard being is union with Hirn,they would be in communion with each other at one comronn altar. He prkyed that God would refresh them with His own presence. and preserve them in His most holy love. His last words would be to the young men—Let the spiritual realities of the Gospel be yours. Be real and manly r Have you made your vows unto God ? Let your life witness to the reality of your conviction. Whatever you believe, in the name of ei o d . live an to your creed. There are neople here to-night of different ways of thinking, of different ways of life. It will make little difference whether we go out of this world Anglicans, Wesleyans. or Catholics, or what not, but it will make an awful difference whether we go into eternity real or not. It will make little difference what our name was. We shall not be judged as to the char- acter of the church on whose roil our name steod,but we shall he jadged asto tke character we bore. Let us pre- pare by faith in Christ, by honest thought, by spiritual aspiration, and step forth into the invisible futuro. with faces Zieuward, and enter upon the future with all its possibilities with quiet and peaceful hearts, and God.eyer ear own God,' will weave the tangled ques- tions of our days and years into an immortal epic et everlasting glory.

div.head: ROBERTS.
div.p: ROBERTS.
An Appointment in Leicester.

Widespread regret has been occasioned by the -parture from the Warrington Wesleyan Circuit, o Rev Rev G. Roberts, M.A., who left this town Thurs lay to talre up an important appointment Leicezt ,r. During his three years' ministry in the circuit,the rev gentleman has gained the esteem 01 all who bave COMB into contact with him,
Ind will _ carry away th 4 be wishes of those
Among whom he has worked. Some details av to lir Roberts's previous career will doubtless be of in- !erest to our readers. The rev _gentleman received

- la theological , training at Beadingley College, Leede, and in 1892 was ordained at Bradford. In t ta.me year, 1892, he was invited to a church in tslemingham and from that town he proceeded to ,I Aew Ferry.Bieltenhead. This was his last appoint- ! ,ftent prior to coming to Warrington. His ministry at „ aew Ferry was most successfuLand the ray. gentle- :. was also closely assoCiatedwith Port Sunlight i being the first Nonconformist minister to preach lk In the village. On leaving the circuit, Mr Roberts Nyae the recipient at a public meeting of an illumi- bated address and purse of gold, subscribed for by „ftembers of all the churches, including the Roman I,atholic. The Vicar of the parish wrote express- M 3 aleuiration of Mr.' Roberts's work, and' said toe good feeling which existed among the religi- "°,4,l bodies in the district was one of the happiest /Nits of his labours and would do much to atrengthen the hands of all in the common cause skeinst the comma enemy. A prominent member of the Roman Cowman Church wrote referring to the good work done by Mr Roberts,of whiab he had %en a witness. The rev gentleman came to Wer- Ongton in leeptemeer, 1898 and was we!comed at a heating of the congregation. He has proved him- self an eloquent preacher. and has discoursed oPon a variety of social topics, the housing of the Daor being a subject upon which he holds very pro- nounced tewe. Me has now been placed in charge of the Belgrave Viresleyan Church. Leiceeter, whine is to be conducted on modern minaion lines. The Sisreh buildings are tt e most commodious in Leicester, and a griet many departments or church Work are in active operation. The 6unday school scholars number over a :..housand. FAREWELL SERMON AT BOLD-STREET CHAPEL. "THE GREAT NEED to THE AGE," MR. ROBERTS'S CONCEPTION OF THE GOSPEL. SUNDAY DEsERVANCE. .„_ Bold-street Wesleyan Church was completely &lied on lelundail eveninv, when the Rev. a. G. Roberts preached Ms larewell sermon Mt elm:negation was in some tesPecto a remarkable one, being comoosed of members of all denominations. The cnoir rendered special music, lilt. Levi Richardson effectively singing the solos. The alati.cm "How lovely are the messengers"(Mendelssores) Was eicoeielly well interpreted. Mr F Hickman ably peesided at the organ. Mr Roberts took for his text Ist Cor., eon 1. 2, 3. and, snsaeing nn the question " Whet ia the Gasoet of Chris. ?" he said that a great deal of norwenrie had often been talked about the preach. , log of the Gosp4, which had been grossly misrepre- 'tented and blasphemously parodied. Many who bon9rtly disbelieved in Christianity were ignorant of the actual nature tf it. They had mistaken its acci- dents for its essence, and acemted for a nortrait what !a only a caricature. All kinds of absurdities and blasphemies had been shouted forch by men suffering under the mad delusion that they were preaching the , Gospel, and thoughtful men had seen in the Christian's 1 . God a Being who as an earthly monarch would not be , tolereted for 12 months, and in the Gospel a set of : doctrines which made life unhappy and death hideous. ' The preacher dwelt upoe the import of the ApostloS decaratioe, erei unfolded tae meaning of the Goepee , arid showed how it was c'-catetisioe with human hie in all its infinite variety. It was no rhetorical exaggera- : tion—nnt the infletel exaegeratinn of an excited Theterse....er, pµF, in the words of Rearm, that to tear the nain • cf Jesus from the world, would be to shake it at ite eery foundation. Voltaire. the Ppen if whose genius Lad not died out of Europe, boasied • that althengh it took lE men to build up Christianity, he Would show that one man could pull it down. ne deep-red that the Gospel was a tissue of fables, fit ordY for cobblers and tailots—though wig such nseful MeMbets a society should be fed on a diet of Hes . Voltaire did rot say. The prediction had hardly been sr ritten before the greatest religious revival and enissionary mevemeet of modern times were in progrers. The logic ot history juAtined them in Raying that the Christian idea was the mightiest force in Eeropean Progress and civilization. In the Chanel they had the solution of the woriii's darke4 prob'ems—Cnristianity Was not a system of barren abstrac.inns which had no Practical bearirg upon the exigencies of He: Some 'People in the town had been a Atte anxious about his '-inception of the' Gospel, and timribin frightened at - times lest the pulpit should he seeularised. He thouebt they would be Ices anxions and efrai i r f the eeculariz- ing of the pulpit if they were more anxious for the 14P1ri1ua1izing of the sectilarities of life. It was not enreogh in these days eimply to repeat the old, ole. story 1 with it many truths as abstract propositions, but to atTly them to the everchangieg circumstances and con- ditions er life. This was the crest need of the age. IheY were on the eve of great things. He was not the ' man to minimise the moral and material grandeur of the British Empire. They had made progress in matters Mslil and religious, such as no other period In history onld parallel, tint it was impossible to close -their eyes to the defects of their virtues and national 1„..7.0e5, and the dangers—the grave dangers— arose from their greattlCßS bnd prosperity. teligion was to an increasing exteast a mere perfunctory 'attendance at some ceremonial which had very little fffect on morals and conscience. There was also a , Xeowine inteferance of all authority and impatierce or testraint. The appetite for pleasure and self-indulgence *as waxing. The sacred and sober duties of home life °Jere being put on one side—a wry serious and signifi- oant sign. Break down the family altar and they des- tped the keystone in the arch nf natural righteousness. me inc neglect of thtiotiservancelef Sunday was „" :.".bOthse signifiCant sign of the times. It was the impera- "lVe duty of the while Catholic Crunch to preach a 4°Bool that would leaven the habits of the people, and oreteet decency in their streets and in their amuse- and at all costs maintain the sanctity of the ntdei Day, and stem the flied of crime and vice which " Ihnes overwhelmed them. Be (the preacher) had ~, ii-adeavourel during his ministry in the town eflu n tdoiorieta4 a gospel—net in vague generalities, b distinctly to the age in which they lived. div.head: PRESENTATION AT PADGATE.
div.p: PRESENTATION AT PADGATE.

Mt ROBERTS conducted the week-night service at the Werreyan Church, Padgate, on Tuesday, when there oast I large congregation. At the concluairm of his ser- mit he thanked all present for the kindness which they had shown him during his ministry in the district. BA re the congregation separated. Mt WILLIAM BENN'ETT P;id that most of thf on were two e that Mr Roberts had been with them three years, and during that period he had wrn their high esteem. It seemed to him nnly Yesterday since he came amongst them, time fl.,w so rapidly, and it was always a source lof regret when their preachers left them, as in the pre- Ent CAPP.

_ Mr JOHN BENNETT and Mr EDWIN RICHARDSON EISO spoke. Mr JOHN E RICHARDSON, i 3 making the nreaentation, referred to the eff vts which the rev. gentleman had marleon behalf of the young peoele of the congreeation, and handed a combined dressing case and travelling bag to him.

The Rev H G ROBERTS, Wirt was tiOTPI2 by surprise said he felt unworthy of their appreciation. He had tried, however. not Maly to serve the interests of the Methodist Chutelt in the district, but also the interests of humanity. He was afraid that his attitude in regard to that phase of life had not been understood. I was a great joy to know that they had apprebiatrd his atti- tude with regard to mane of the questions that he had touched anon dpring hia ministry in the circuit. He was one of those who believed that the Gospel was too great and majestic for ene church to make a monopoly of, and he felt that if they were to touch the masses of the people they must preach a sympathetic Gospet.and mast hold out to them the sympathies of the Lord Jesus (Inlet. Be had always felt that Palgate was his home. _ _

(Gear. hear. and applause ) Might God bless and refresh them. lie hoped they would show his successor the same loran), they showed to him and might the church at Padgate go forward as " fair as the moon, Sc clear as tie u n and as strong as an army with barnere." (Heer:hear, and applause.) The proceedings closed with the singing of the Doxology.

div.head: WARRINGTON ANGLERS' ASSOCIATION. Second Match.
div.p: WARRINGTON ANGLERS' ASSOCIATION. Second Match.

The second contest in connection witli the above Society wag decided in the waterg of the River Weaver, at Vale Royal. on Saturday afternoon last. There was a record entry of 93 as compared with 77 laat year. Under the able management of Messrs. P Knight, eeneral seer try ; Mr F I Ernson, assi.tant secretary ; A Cook, H Kent, W H Gandy and N Unsworth, all the arrangements made, worked admirably, not a single bitch occurring. The rule " that no contestant be allowed to wet a line on the day prior to the contest " was much approved of. The length of canal chosen for the match extended a distance of nearly 1,000 yards, and it was an interestine sight to we so many anglers congregated toi2ether. Prompt to time 3.15 p.m., the draw commenced and at 3.40 p.m. "time " was called to begin operations. The fishing was limited to two hours. but as the time progressed it was apparent that not great amount of sport was being recorded, which was contrary to entinipation. At the conclu- sion of the allotted time, weighing the catches commenced and to facilitate matters in this direction two pairs of scales had been acquired and Otis this important part of the proceedings was speedily accomplished. div.head: FREE CHURCHES.
div.p: THE FREE CHURCHES.
GIPSY SMITH'S AUTOBIOGRAPHY.

This will undoubtedly be one of the most icteresting books to be published diming the coming season, We understand that Mr. Smith is now hard, at work on ;the volume, which is to be issued by the National Free Church Council in the middle of :November. It will contain many illustrations, of rare and curious interest.' As everyone • knows, Gipsy Smith has had a romantic career. Ilekv4l tell the full story with great wealth. of picturesque detail in this volume. Mr. Smith is, at the present moment, perhaps. the Most , popular evangelist in the English-speaking World, and we fully expect that his book will sell by thousands.

div.head: METHODIST (ECUMENICAL CONFERENCE.
div.p: THE METHODIST (ECUMENICAL CONFERENCE.

The Conference is the most interesting coming event in Nonconformity. The services are to be held in Wesley's Chapel, City-road, and the great men of Methodism from all parts of the world will be in attendance. Some of the subjects to be. (..liscussed are rather large, but this is quite in, harmony with the nature of the gathering. The National Free 'Church Council, tho United iFtee 'Church. of Scotland, and the' Salvation Army ere the uly in*Stitu- tions which are to be allowed to obtrude upon the deliberations of .the Conference. The depu- tation from the National Council Will consist of Dr. Parker, Dr. Monro Gibson, Dr. Clifford, and Mr. George Cadbury outside Methodism four of the..tnost. notable ainong Free Churchmen.

div.head: PEBLItAN AND THE EVANGELIST.
div.p: THE PEBLItAN AND THE EVANGELIST.

The Rev. Jesse Mayo, who is in charge of the Free Church Council's Mission Van, at present touring in Surrey, is having some remarkable experiences. At Lodsworth the van was pitched in the centre of the village, ten paces from the public-house door. The missioner looked right into the drinking-bar and spoke to the men who were drinking there, just as he might from a pulpit. The public-house pro- prietor was exceptionally kind, and provided the people with seats from his own bar room.

div.head: MR. ALFRED DAVIES, M.P.
div.p: MR. ALFRED DAVIES, M.P.

This well-ynown Nonconformist Member of Parliament has been attracting considerable attention of late. He has won a great reputa- tion in the House by his pertinacity as a ques- tioner of Mr. Chamberlain, and by his humour. In personal appearance Mr. Davies strongly resembles the immortal Mr. Pickwick, as the photograph in the September Free Church Chronicle makes very plain. He is a member of Dr. Horton's congregation at Lyndhurst- road, Hampstead, and was one of the original deacons. Mr. Davies is one of the merriest, and at the same time one of the shrewdest, of men. He started business on his own account as an international carrier and underwriter when he was only twenty-one, and now his firm has branches in all 'parts of the world. He takes a great interest in the housing of the poor, and no slum landlord has a more relentless and more unsleeping enemy than Mr. Davies. The Colonial Secretary, whom Mr. Davies is continually baiting, is on the best of terms with his tormentor.

div.head: COATLESS -CONGREGATION.'
div.p: A COATLESS -CONGREGATION.'

The heat has been very great in America. One Sunday recently when the Rev. John McNeil preached in Pittsburg, Pennsylvania, the temperature was 96deg. in the shade. Fifty per cent of the men in the congregation had come without their coats, and on being inviteti to make themselves as comfortable as possible, the remainder rose in a body and removed theirs. Many men on this timid side of the water would like to follow this inspiring example, but most of us less daring Britishers have not the pluck of our cousins
"HARRY LINDSAY."

Mr. H. Lindsay Hudson (" Harry Lindsay of Methodist Idylls fame), who recently re- signed the editorship of the Methodist Weekly, has now settled at Glossop. He has a fine pro- spect of the Derbyshire moiri tains from his study windows, and is happy at being far away from noise and smoke. Messrs. Chatto and Windus are to bring out Mr. Hudson's historical romance, entitled "Judah Pycroft, Puritan," which rasi as a serial through the Methodist Times. The late editor has also written some liyely papers on his journalistic experience.

div.head: REV. W. K. BURFORD, SHEFFIELD.
div.p: REV. W. K. BURFORD, SHEFFIELD.

The resignation of Mr. Burford, who for thirteen years was pastor of Wicker Church, was received with great regret in the cutlery city: The health of Mrs. Burford necessitates her immediate, removal to the South of Ang- land. Mr. Burford has been a successful and beloved pastor and preacher, and, as those who have read his little work on "Wayside Angels" are aware, he has literary gifts of no mean order. He is widely read, full of enthusiasms, tender and powerful. We are confident that he will soon find a sphere of labour in a locality suitable to his wife's health.

div.head: REV. J. TOLEFREE PARR.
div.p: REV. J. TOLEFREE PARR.

On August 31 this popular Primitive Methodist minister begins work as the third missioner of the National Free Church Council at Mexboro'. Mr. Parr's mission colleagues are Gipsy Smith and Mr. W. R. Lane. The new evangelist's chief qualification for his work is that he has already done a great deal of similar work and that successfully. During his last mission at Norwich the Agricultuaal Hall, which holds four thousand people, was crowded every night. Mr. Parr is forty-0x years of age, though he looks younger, and has toiled hard all his life. His first work was in a shipping office in Liverpool.

div.head: ANGLICAN CATHEDRAL AT CAPE TOWS.
div.p: THE ANGLICAN CATHEDRAL AT CAPE TOWS.

We observe that the Duke of York has just laid the foundation stone of the new Cathedral at Cape Town. We sincerely hope that this enterprise will be carried to a speedy and suc- cessful conclusion. At the same time we trust that the Anglican dignitaries will abandon the unworthy tactics of seeking money for this fabric on the ground that it is to be a national memorial to those who have fallen in the war. The Rev. C. H. Kelly, Acting-President of the, National Council, and the Rev. Thomas,Law the Organising Secretary, have shown con- clusively in a fetter to the Press that the Cathe- dral could not have any such character. For one thing, the Church of England. in Cape Colony occupies an altogether inferior position compared with other communions. The latest official figures are:
