div.head: FRIOAY, AUGUST 30 1901
div.p: FRIOAY, AUGUST 30 1901
!MR. A. H. CROSFIELD ON THE WAR.
SUPPLEMENTARY LETTER.

The Cost of the war. [the following letter from Mr erolifield should have reached us in time for publication in our last issue, but owing to a inisehawe we did [LA receive it tilt this week.— editor, Rik:4lllER Sir,—Tue figures in the following estimate of the cost of the war are taken from a book which I have ventured to call the best abilling'a-worthepub- listed for many a day and from which I have already quoted in preceding letters. In brief corn- pars Mr Methuen has given us in his book "Peace or War" a s:atement of all the essential facts relat- ing and leading up to the rioath African imbroglio which is as masterly as (excepting only some criti- cisms of military questions which might have been left out) it is unanswered and unanswerable. One of the most ‘aluabla chapters in this book is entitled " Government without Consent." It is from this lam about to quote Cu show the future burden of debt and taxation we have piled up, and are still piling up for ourselves. Mr Methuen shows that the expenditure of the two Republics was at its highest about .24,000,000—but under the more sfacieut and more costly English rule which we shall inaugurate at the conclusion of the war this figure will probably stand at £6,ooo,ooo—and that is wiihout making by any means an ex:ravagant estimate. Then, when the submission of the Boers is in- forced and the war comes to an end, there will be the expense of the Mounted Police, a force of 10,000 men at a salary of £2OO por annum, per man, which with the additional cost of extra allowances, rations, horses and equipment for the rank and file, and allowing for the high cost of all neces- saries of life out there, will amount he calculates to at least another .1:2 a week per man. The cost of this police force therefore in pay and keep is put at £3,000,000 per annum—then of course it will as he says be necessaty for some years to maintain a large force of say at least 4,000 men in the con- quered territories, the cost of weica be works out at £5,000,000 per annum. this gives us a total expenditure of £14,000,000. That there is good reason for not calculating on the Transvaal and Orange River Colony raising more than a fourth of this amount will be gathered from the fact that previous to the war the revenue of the two countries was about £4,800.000. of this the Transvaal Government received £250,000 per annum from the mines. In the following cal- culation that amount is doueled. There are a good many people who would not cry their eyes out if in the near future t!..is contribu- tion from the mines was trebled or quadrupled, but Mr J B Robinson and other mine-owners have, during the last few months, vehemently protested against the placing of any heavier burdens on the mines, and the iofl uence and the power of the mine- owners and the n-msssity of their co-operation with the ltne,lish Government will force us to yield to their wishes and to spare the mines any burden much heavier than they bore under the Trausvaal Government. In 1898 the aggregate amount of ! dividends paid by the gold mines was under .C 5,000000 . . . and making every allowance for an increased output of gold and lighter burdens, it will be impossible for the English Government to raise from the gold mines much more than .£500,000 a year. In addition to the sources of revenue which we have given above, there remain a few " conces- sions Or mining rights which, having been the property of the Transvaal Republic, will plas into the bands of its successors. The value of these rights has been exaggerated, and they probably will not realsse more than £2,000,000, which. at 4 per cent., will yield an income of £BO.OOO a year. This last figure may :be under the mark ; at any rate we are teld that these concessions will yield a good deal more. Well, Mr Methuen's estimate of which he says that it must in the nature of things be rough, though it will probably be found that the aggregate amounts are not far distant from the truth, is as follows :

div.head: RELEIPTS.
div.p: RELEIPTS.
4. Taxation of gold mines 500,00 e) 1 rn volts .. 1,000,000 Nttherlands railway 750,000 Income from sales of new concessions. Dues and licences 750 000 Post office Other receipts
£3,650,000 FXPENDITURE.
Civil administration of the
two provinces .. 6008,000 Military occupation Police lorce of 10,000 men

Deficit £10,350,009 Mr Methuen continues it is possible and probable that this disastrous balance-sheet will be improved in the course of years, but no material improvement is pos-ible while a military occupation of the two territories is necessary. Tne capital expense of the war mug be met by some sort of loan, whether wholly by an addition to the national debt of England, or partly by a loan to the New colonies under British guarantee. But the result will be the same. The interest on the money will and can only he paid by the English taxpayer. If the war is continued for a further considerable periedits capital expense will amount at least to £225,000,000 which will be increased to £250,000,000 if we assume that a special loan of £25,000,000 will be necessary for the restoration of agriculture and the rebuilding of the burnt farms. The interest on this amount allowing for a sinking fund, at 3.,} per cent will be £8,750,000, and if we add this amount to the &licit on the revenue accounts of the two States i.e. £10,350,000, we arrive at a total of over £19,000,000. Such is the annual burden which our new Colonies will lay upon us for some years if we determine to secure the submission cf the inhabitants by military methods and to control their disaffection by the sword. When Charles Booth produced his scheme for old age pensions by which everyone 65 years of age or more was to receive 5s per week (apart from some difference of opinion as to the wisdom of putting everyonelwithout discriminal ion on a level footing) the country was a bit staggered at the annual cost which was put at about .C 17,000,090. We have new practically let ourselves in for additional taxation for that amount, and more— which be it sooner or be it later has to be faced—and old age pensions (on which the Government came into office in '95). —Whera:are they? They served Mr Chamberlain's purpose at the last general election but one, and I now he has washed his hands of them. It to all this our Tory friends object that a war which in the first instance was just and necessary eoes not become the reverse because it costs a lot of money no one will differ with them. There has been no wavering that I kuoys of about supplying the men and means for all this vast expenditure of blood and treasure. What is condemned is the policy which led up to the war and those further errors of polity and judgment which have kept it going, But then all the evidence goes to show that this promise has no foundation in fact : that the War was in the first place entirely unnecessary and in the second might have been stopped in the early stages, had we given the Boers a fair chance to climb down. It was the Govesnment's insistence for so long on unconditional surrender which aggravated the mischief to such a frightful extent. In the above figures no allowance is made for the possible dangers ahead of us in Cape Colony and we may devoutly hope there is need for none. But we have to reckon with and recognise the fact that to some-extent the loyalty of the Cape Dutch has been undermined. Their sympathy with the Boers ol the Transvaal and the Orange River Colony is not political but racial. " The same blood," writes Mr Methuen, "flows in their veins, they are related by ties of marriage and kin- ship, and the sympathy which they fee for two peoples of the same blood is the sympathy which ICnolishmen would feel under the same con- ditions for men of their blood threatened with annihilation by a great Power" The Dutch Colon- ists had not shown before the Jameson raid any I violent sympathy with the Transvaal ; on the Other band, they had displayed considerable hostility to- wards the political defects of the Boer Government. They recognised too well the advantages of their position as an English Colony to wish to join their political fortunes with those of the Trani,vaal. (Methuen p. 173.) Further on speaking of the Cape Dutch he continues, "With the exception of the in- habitants of Caps Town, under martial law, which

in fact the negation of all law, they are liable o punishment if they stir out of their houses after the time of curfew, if they make a jesting remark to an English soldier. Their horses are taken from ' them,their cattle,their forage, and even their boots. Their papers are suppressed,their editors imprisonei their parliament is indefinitely prorogued, and all , their representative rights are in abeyance. Can we I wonder if their loyalty to the English Throne has in this chilling atmosphere grown cold ? " Protest enough there was against the policy that in the end drove the Orange River Colony into making CDmmon cause with the Transvaal against us. Common sense let alone statesmanship might have taught us this was the very thing to avoid. Is it possible that we may go one worse "by unit- ing a large number of the Cape Dutch against us? Fortunately the Colony has thriven so well under Imperial Government that this dire calamity has not yet darkened political skies that are sombre enough without it. But we are taking great risks ; and the fiarsh overbearing uncompromising spirit which Chamberlain displays in his speeches heals no woands and pours no oil on the waters of those troubled Southern Seas. Brow beating, and the tactics of the American boss may have answered pretty well in Birmingham politics, and it may have paid to put the screw on there. But these things are a sorry sort of training for a man who has to deal with international problems demanding breadth of mind, high impartiality, and a dignity of character which commands respect and confidence and is incapable of in any degree sacrificing national interest for the sake of scoring off some antagonir. Energy, courage, capacity, we all know Mr Chamberlain and Lord Milner possess and these are qualities which command ad- miration and respect, but something more was needed to settle this question, and of the wisdom "which"says Johnson "comprehends at once the end and the means, estimates easiness or difficulty, and is ceutious and confident in due proportion" they have shown none; no far-sighted, broad-minded tolerance; not even the homely faculty of what is called putting yourself in his place. Is not this same faculty badly needed now on all hands? In high places at least there must be a woeful lack of itnazination or we should realize better the sort of legacy this evil work will leave behind it. Do they ever atop to think what would be the consequence in England if some invading foe not content with beating the Army and the Government, set to work to crush the nation and, in order to do this, on one pretext or another bariat houses. forms, and stores, looted and destroyed property of all de- scription, and as a consequence of this decimated women an children by the insanitary wretched- ness of concentration camps with a mortality in some of them equal to that of Bombay in the plague. Assume what in the present struggle we know to be the case, that these sufferings were mitigated as far as ever circumstances allowed, by the chivalry and kindheartedness of the invading forcea. Would that reconcile Englishmen to all the physical and mental anguish and despair for the very young as for those who are old or frail "sweeping" i.e. devastating a country in this way involves? Chamberlain hinted that the complaint that children faded and died like wi, hered flowers under this system was " irrelevant." Would the mothers think it so in England and would they counsel the men fighting in defence of their coun- try to accept an abject and disgraceful uncondi- tional surrender? No more than they have done in South Africa and his attempt to drive them to it is brute force and tyranny of the worst description. The policy Burke condemned in the American War as impious then, is impious now. This was not what Lord Kitchener wanted. Mr Chamber- lain's arguments in his speech last Friday that the Boers would listen to nothing short of absolute in- dependence are so thin and so transparently shallow that everyone sees through them. The simple fact remains that Botha did show his willingness to discuss terms with Lord Kitchener of which the latter made incorporation of the Republics in the Empire the startling point and a sine Tria non. If some of my Liberal friends object that we have no moral right to take these countries I respect- fully submit that in the first place there are two sides to that propositicn (though I for one wou'd not particularly care to argue its converse) and in the second place even if our title deeds were diffi• cute to prove on grounds of strict morality in politics we have to work not for an ideal ethical abstraction but for what is practical and possible. Apart from other very strong arguments in favour of annexation it is perfectly plain that in the pres•lit temper of the nation no settlement unless based on annexation would be listened to in Eng- land.

In these letters on the War I have said very little of the Government's actual conduct of affairs nor will I begin now for the letters are too long as it is. Otherwise from a mere party point of view the subject is tempting enough in all conscience. The Cabinet's ignorance and the mutual contradictions by its members on the subjeets of Boer armarbents! the telegram to the Colonies" unmounted troops preferred ;" the announcementi (I think about two months after the fighting began) that we as little expected to be at War with tho Orange Free State as with Switzerland ! and all the rest of it— This was summed up aptly enough by Lord Rose- bery in his spirited speech the other day. Speaking of tie Government's management(?) of affairs from first. to last be exclaimed—Oh! my heavens is the Ananias yet born who will defend them ? My object in writing these letters however, has not been mainly to criticise administration. What I've tried to do is to investigate the excuses offered in extenuation of this War and to compare them with the causes that really led up to it and the policy which has kept it going. To recapitulate a few of the most important, I have shown that it is nonsense to shift the respon- sibility on to Mr Gladstone's shoulders. We should have heard nothing more against his s-ttlement of 1881—which, by the way, Mr Chamberlain was the first to insist on with his characteristic energy and which also had the support of more moderate men like Lord Hartington and Lord Darby—but for dis- covery of gold in 1885. Not that this again and the influx of Uitlanders was the slightest excuse or occasion for the war. The Jameson Raid was the first step towards it but time was repairing the consequences of that piece of brigandage, bad as it was, and made worse by the way in which the con- spir- ey was condoned and hushed up, and the mov- ing spirit afterwards honoured and complimented in England. Even that in no way made war inevitable. But it was then the few very rich,very powerful,wholly unscrupulous and un-English meni who engineered the Raid a second time showed the Dutch the cloven hoop. Subsequently they worked up and worked upon race prejudices through their press, sought to set the British against the Dutch and with the same object nobbled Lord .Milner and converted him into a thorough-paced partisan. How far he influenced and on the other hand was influenced by Mr Chamberlain is a personal issue which however interesting we are not in a position to decide. Wnat we do know is that he ed the game of the men who not content with the Raid were still plotting the overthrow of the Transvaal,and that the organs in the English press which unfortunately most accurately represent the views of this unprin cipalled gang publicly thanked heaven that PO late as August, '99 we had so narrowly escaped a peace- ful settlement.

Some of our Tory friends brush all this aside as rut history. Why waste time over it they say ? Let bygones be bygones. Of course, so does every sinner. But if a minister, or a cabinet, trading on the f%htiag spirit which still fortunately exists in _ _

Fngh;ncl, ready to defend the empire in any real bona fide emergency that arises, are to feel that he or they, can land us in any war with impunity on the principal of standing to win everything if it is just and popular—lose nothing if it is proved to be the reverse, we ar3 in a decidedly precarious condition. In that case we should fully need the friendly advice from Mr Carnegie in the "I9:h Century" where he warns us in our Imperial policy to" let sleeping dogs lie and cut our coat according to our cloth." We must have no more of knell recklees and ruinuous work and the best way to eheek it is to take care that the responsibility for it is settled on the right shoulders. But if we take our friends at their word and turn from the past to the present what is it that first strikes us. Surely it, is the lesson which John Bright taught years ago in that famous aphorism now so brought hams to us, Applicable in all cases it may net be, but never did history prove more clearly than recent events in South Africa that of itself and by itself "force is no remedy." P.S. But for a mischance this letter written about a fortnight since should have reached you long ago. Since then we have had several notice- able events. First the interview with Mr Kruger published in the Paris " Figaro " which has been hailed by our War-at-any-price. Fight-to-a-finish, organs in the Press as proving that any settlement is impracticable. It proves nothing of the kind. But it Roes to show that history is repeating itself ; and that as in the war with the American Colonies

so now the more desperate we make the Boers the less easy does a settlement become, and the greater the responsibility if those who have thrown away invaluable opportunities of coming to terms with the enemy. Secondly the Government has authorised the 'issue of another proclamation, much milder than I some of the 40 other proclamations that have pre- ceded it, but threatening certain penalties to any Boers still in arms after September 15th, and banishment for the leaders. They must be sanguine people who think men like Botha and De Wet unde- terred by more drastic pronlamatiens last year,will be driven to sue for peace by threats of this kind : weak threats in which "I dare not" obviously waits upon " I would." The rd event—though one of less moment —to which I will refer, is a vigorous speech of the usual kind by the Colonial Secre- tary. At the conclusion of that speech be asks his friends, foregathered in full force at Blenheim, to go home and' once more spread the light in all districts of Great Britain and to explain and make clear the great issues for which we have been fighting, &c." Is not this like inviting the blind to lead the blind. Of the various excuses for the war given to the public at different stages would it not have been as well for Mr Chamberlain to tell his audience which is to be considered the authorised version.

If any of our Tory friends are now about to un- bosom themselves on this obscure—and rather deli- cate—question, will they at. the same time answer another kindred question ; of putting every other consideration on one side, will they tell us, if one may ask for a straight answer to a straight ques- tion, whether they, who two years ago thirsted for war, now consider that the game was worth the caudle ? Yours, etc., St. Moritz, August 20, 1901.
A. IL CROSFIELD.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Cricket.

It was unfortunate that Alf Thewlis, the popular Warrington professional, was unable to appear in the match set apart for his " benefit " last Saturday. A., the last moment it became known that the " pro" could not take the field owing to indisposition, and naturally much disappointment was felt. The visiting team was Manchester who came down to Arpley with a team largely made up of professionals. The Warring- ton eleven was not constituted as it was originally intended it should be, H Tinsley, an old pro- fessional of the Warrington Club, who had promised to assist, being unable to make the :hurnev from Leyland. As I have before stated, Thewlis was indisposecLand the vacancies were filled by A Thompson and A Duckworth. The City eleven ran out easy victors, compiling 172 to the home team 107.

Warrington won the toga, and batted first,the opening batsmen, E A Connor and Dr Smith, being oppcsNi Sladen and G Littlewood. Connor soon gor to work and scored freely off Slade°, making '25 out of 30 before he woo taken at the wicket:With the addition of a single,J Callon failed to reqpnril to a call from Dr Smith,and the initial batsman failed to regain his crease. J Call^n and J Brigge batted steadily, and took the total to 37, when lunch was taken. Resuming, each batsman got Sladen away to the boundary, hut a floe ball from the fast bowler disturbed Callon'a leg stump.

Four runs later Brigs was bowled,and B Si!cock and J Gibbon became associated. Steady play ensued, and tho score had reacbed 60, when J Littlewond relieved Sladen. The separation came from the other end, for a fine bill from G Littlewood completely teat Cr,bbon. Another disaster followed, for at the sam. total Sdcock jumped out to drive J Littlewood, and fell a victim to Radcliffe's dexterity behind the stumps.

J W Bibby commenced in promising style, whilst the first ball H a.mpaon received he lifted to . the boundary. At 76 the Warrington captain was bowled in playing forward. Useful contributions were made by Thomp- son and Duckworth, whilst Hasapson played the bowl- ing with confidence. Tha innings closed for 107, !lampoon carrying out his bat far a faultless 17.

Manchester were first represented by E S Harrison and Holland, E A Connor and E Gits,n sharing the bowling. From the start the bawling was played vridi ease, and runs came freely. Holland was missed from a hard drive at 41, and profiting by this escape, drove each bowler to the confines. At 43 a double change was tried, J Gibbon and Dr Smith taking up the attack. The total stood at 75, when Harrison was cauThr. by Hampson, standing well back, whilst ten runs later Holland was smartly run out. Harry had hut a brief stay, for after making five he was palpably leg before to Dr Smith. A Lyon and Wtight passed the Warring- ton score, bit at 109 Wright return.d one to Gibbon, A useful stand was made br tilt brothers Littlewood and the innings closed for 172.
Cycling. AE Howard, of Warrington, competed in the mile bicycle race at Leigh St. Joaeph's sports rva Saturday and accured third position with a start of 170 yards.

Another cycle accident is to be added to the long list which has taken plaie on the brow near Lymm Church. On Sunday a youth, whn WRS apparently an unexperi- enced rider was clmiog down the big when be les?, control of his machine. He was told to keep straight on, but cluirl not manh,go his machine and was thrown heavily, with the rerult that his knee cap was badly injured. He was also severely bruised.

Foot Racing. E Harris, ths well-known Warrington footballer, is coming into prominence as a sprinter, and seored a further suzcess at the Leigh St. JosPah's sperts held on Saturd-v. Harris ran in third in 100 yards open race with 834 yards start, inches only separating him from his more successful competitors.—ln the 220 yards local race,. Bramelew, of Leigh, ran first, while Arthur Holland, of Warrington, was placed second, both run- ning from the scratch mark. Holland led until a few yards rff the rope, when Bromelow went fast to win. The judge refused to put the numbers up. stating that there had been " roping" and that the case would have to go before the A. A.A.
Great Sankey School Board—No Continuation
Classes.

This Board held its monthly meeting on Tuesday evening. Mr F Halton presiding. There were also present: —Messrs Halton (chairman), Fulton Smith, Perks, Kilshaw, Wright, and George Clarke (head- master). It, was reputed that there was a balance in hand in fav3ur of the Board of £22 Os 10d. Ur Clarke presented a report showing that there had been no attendance for the weeks ending August 3, 10, and 17 owing to the holidays. For the week ending August 24 the names of 306 children were on the books, of which 271 had been in attendance. the average being 245.5. The fees paid amounted to 12s 6d. The attendance last week was not as high ash might have been,and it had not improved much this week. Letters were read from Miss Wright and Miss Saunders resigning their posi- tions as assistant mistresses of the school. It was decided to accept the resignations. Mr Clarke said he bad not had a moment's uneasiness on account ci the assistant-mistresses during the past three years. The Chairman: It is a pity they are going. (Hear, hear.) It was decided to advertise for suc- cessors each at a salary of £45 a year, or according to qualification. The headmaster said a circular had been received from the Education Department con- cerning the continuation classes. It was for the Board to decide whether they should be continued this year. It was decided on the motion ot the Chairman, to discontinue the classes during the next twelve months

A. DISTINGUISHED The Clergy and the Press, preacher is. never so fortunate in his refer- ences as when he is discoursing to pressmen. He is at his broadest and his best when he addresses those who are really his fellow-ministers to the advanoenaent of the race. The sermon preached by the BISHOP of RIPON at Leeds to the Institute of Journalists takes high ground, and it is, there- fore, the more likely to be appreciated, not only by the journalists themselves, but by the vast body of people who are the daily witnesses of the work which the Press performs in 'the interest of humanity. The three-fold claim which the Bishop put forward as the birthright of man is but a new form of an old and valuable sentiment, and to put it forward from the pulpit in the terms in which it was set forth by the right rev, prelate is a wise exercise of discretion, and likely to form a strong bond of sympathy between true men in both pro- fessions. A man's title to full possession of his powers is a raditil principle that lies at the root of all civilization, and of the many beneficent measures which that term implies. When it is realised,:as his lordship'puts it, that the first desideratum in life is that of self-expres- sion, when the key is found to what will change human existence on this sublunary plane from the mean, sordid thing that it is to something divine in its essence and aspiration, for, given the postu- late that human character is the expression of the individual in a certain set of circumstances, and, therefore, properly the expression of the divine spark in the individual, then it follows that the man has something to live for beyond the mere material things of a day, that perish in the using. A more fitting word in season could not have been addressed to the journalists thm. that offered by the BISHOP in this connection'. After pointing out that some could speak but could not hear, while others had great ideas, great thoughts, but could not or did not give them utterance, he described the few—the chosen ones—who hear the voices that sound around them—now the voice of the prophet, now the voice of advancing knowledge, now the voice of highest duty, now the voice of GOD; and they could speak and interpret for their fellow-men. This is au apt dAlineation alike of the true journal- ist, the true preacher and teacher,,the true writer and sayer of things to the people. It is a high ideal for all so engaged, but it is not too high for the aspiration of all who desire to excel in the god- like work of leading men te Divine wisdom, by a knowledge of themselves and the things that con- cern them. The second head in the Bisnor's claim is no less pregnant in stimulating sugges- tion. A man's position in society, by which is not meant the usual acceptation of the latter term on its shallow side, is the measure equallj of his privilege and his responsibility under the law of love, the law of service, the law of bratherhood. The rule of life which shall survive will not be the sordid rule of selfishness which the worship lof Mammon has set up, but the altruistic cultiva- tion of one's gift, and its devotion to the service

of one's fellow-man. Where aociety gives sca ntill to the individual little may be expected in return of altruistic devotion, though the history of the world has shewn great exceptions. Or it may be reasoned that where the individual gives little society—that is, the individuals in the mass—Wlll
recognise its responsibility the less. Therefore practically it is difficult to see wkere or how the

action of a principle so beneficent is to begin. But needless to waste time speculating, for has itS operation not already begun in the many bright individual examples which have already left their impress on organised society? Society is alreadY reciprocating, and although the contest with the lower elements which retard is a bard one, and the odds seem very much against the survival Of what:worldly wisdom regards as foolishness, and, indeed, few understand, yet the principle is the w' principle of life, of progress, and it must conquer. In the Blencre's third head, the inheritance Of freedom, the preacher struck the oldest,truest and most powerful note in his trichord. Freedom of thought and expression—freedom of opinion,tree- dom of the Press, civil and religious liberty—is' the charter which progressives and reformers have upheld as the sine qua non ever since men under- stood progress. A valuable contribution to the subject is the BISHOP'S admission that those in 'authority in Church as well as State "had some- ' times hesitated" to grant the free expression necessary to development, " through a fear that was injustice, and had made a mistake" in se doing. The great TEACHER of Nazareth pointed out the mistake long ago, so the Bailor reminds us. But men prefer to find out their errors by ex- perience—bitter sometimes, but effectual. They are now finding out, slowly but thoroughly. It is a sign of the times, and a hopeful one.

The pastoral prepared at The Wesleyan Pastoral, the direction of the recent Wesleyan Conference, and now issued under the signatures of the esteemed president and secretary of the body, is a document that will appeal to a large constituency, even out' side of the denomination itself. As one of the oldest of the English Nonconformist bodies, whose testimony has ever been for liberty and spiritu- ality, the verdict of the Methodist Connexion oa - the signs of the times is one of singular interest. It is true that in one sense theirs is a narrow plat- form; but it has always been the strait gate and the narrow way that led to righteousness and CO progress. Its average of sincerity is, perhaps!, greater than most, and if it has erred ;n
I

and its disregard of general culture it is 120 above mending its ways. The pastoral takes due note of the struggle which has closed the century, in which forces intellectual and critical, as well as material, have taken part with the result, in the former case, that satis- faction seems to be expressed, although, surelYt it cannot be regarded as final or conclusive' It is something to know that the "foundation of God standeth sure " ; but when the authors of the pastoral tell us that "from the furnace of historical criticism into which it had been cast tbs
New Testament has come loosed from the thongs

of tradition, made ready for wider service, and for more confident appeal by the witness of fire to its proof," one is in doubt whether to congratulate them on the advanced and intelligent standpoint they have reached or to ask them if they are avail.° of all that it involves. The sanction of traditioll has been largely the basis upon which the jp(o;iain claims of the Scriptures to then-Thique posit.% as the standards of the Christian Churches hay- rested. Are the Methodists, then, prepared t° dispense with it, and for the future try the New Testament, as they would any other written authority, by the" witness of fire," which we take to be the,inner witness of man's highest conscious- ness ? If that is the position deliberately assumed, the Methodists are to be congratu- lated on its highly spiritual basis. It mai have its practical difficulties, but these may safelY be left to take care of themselves, though the de- velopments at times may be startling. The pas'
I
I

toral deplores the increase of materialism which it' so apparent on every hand. But, with curious in' consistency, it has just made something of a boast of having got together the sum of £920,000 Wtb which to start the century. It would appear tO recognise the fact that even spiritual work caw:lop be carried on without very material assistance

from material sources, and the denomination sr parently knows the art of making friends of the Mammon of unrighteousness. So long as Mare' mon is so indispensable even to the existence and the work of Churches, so long will it be Wl' shipped, and its worship tolerated by those whose mission it is to set higher things before the mind° of men as objects of attainment. Perhaps this is what the Methodists propose to do—now thei have got the Mammon.

Particularly sad are the circumstances attend' ing the drowning of a Warrington youth at he- trobus on Sunday morning. He and three companions had started off into the country 0? Saturday evening, and they spent the night 1" Whitley—rather an unaccountable freak unlnge these young fellows are specially fond of fresh for,' The following morning they rambled about, an" the hot sunshine tempted deceased to bathe in e; pit at Antrobus. We are told that he could 110' but could not swim. For a few minutes be appeared to have enjoyed the bathe and then get; ting out of his depth he sank and was drowneo before the eyes of his companions, none of who'll could swim. The lack of knowledge in natatory art is very deplorable, and surpris" ing too, considering the opportunities there, are nowadays for learning to swim. It is a grew' pity that swimming is not made compulsory Or all young people. There would be fewer heart- rending fatalities if there was such an enactment' Even a rudimentary knowledge of swirnnne.g would suffice to save life in many cases, and ever ally in those of the type uuder notice. Mal inbred ignorance of natation is the only point le which he is inferior to the dumb creation, and it is so important that steps ought certainly to be taken to remedy this physical disability.

As all the world knows this tatoous unraveller of mysteries vanished from 'llnlan ken some few years ago—we believe over a Ilr.eeipice--and Dr. Doyle refused to resuscitate At last the persuasions of the publisher have Prevailed, and in last month's" Strand Magazine" ;PPeared the opening chapters of a story with t herlock Holmes as the chief character. Needless Bay, the revival created great inter ast, and 'The „ ound of the Baskervilles,"as the story is called,was :,eltcl with avidity, and found to be in quite the best YlO of both Dr. Doyle and Mr. Sherlock Holmes. he Continuation is found in the September num- :r of the magazine, which is just, out, and the 'r3, is still "to be continued." The heat cl.kci perhaps extended itself to the baronet's Ziaper ; at any rate, he turned away with the ZPIY, "IF you are thirsty, you know where the 7611 is, You will find a pail there." Thinking rer his remark a little later, it flashed across the bar3oet's mind that he had given orders for three io°ttles of champagne to be put into the pail and O'ered into the well to cool for dinner. MATTERS OF MOMENT.
A Provincial Letter.

From many quarters during the week have come stories of storm, damage, and shipwreck. The stranding of an excursion steamer near Guernsey approached alarmingly near to becoming an appall- ing disaster. In the River Severn, near Worcester, two steamers collided in a fog, and here again no personal injdry resulted. Ihus far there was cause for gratitude when the first alarm was over. But not so on the South coast, where the Lusitania, a Spanish vessel, sank, and four persons were drowned. From other districts there were reports of vessels in difficulties, but, on the whole, the results have not been so bad as were at first antici- pated.

Scarcely have the public been allowed to recover from the shock of learning all about skirts that sweep the streets of provincial towns arid cities and their influence on public health, when they are asked to face another distressing problem. From about the ladies' feet to their heads we are asked to look ; where it is said that straw hats are teem- ing with baccili. The gentler sex, intent on keep- ing their hats in pose, plunge large pins through the artistic wonders, and these weapons become covered with the apparently everywhere busy baccili. So that—will it be believed ? —when ladies are getting their hats ready for the stabbing operations, they, or some of them, put their hatpins in their mouths. This is the ever watchful baccili's opportunity, and leads to all manner of perils. At least, so say those who ought to know. Of course, the male reader is not concerned, except as a friend of the endan- gered ()nee. For he will perhaps want toaknow now if an affected hat pin is or is not quite innocuous after it has been furtively used as a pips-cleaner and replaced on a fair one's toilet table! Ile would undoubtedly be glad to have scientific assurance in favour of a very convenient practice, against which, however. a foolish prejudice seems to exist from his point of view.

Electric and other tramway schemes are beard of from all parts of the provinces, and inasmuch as the provinces certainly led the way with electri- cally propelled " trains," it is perhaps not surpris- ing to hear that the London United Tramways Company are now entertaining the idea of, appeal- ing to Parliament next session for the necessary powers to commence a large and comprehensive system of tramways, to work in connection with the existing system. If the present intention be cartied out, as no doubt it will, there is every proi- pect of the company going considerably beyond the metropolitan boundary ; routes to Wimbledon and to Croydon being included in the scheme now under consideration.

Time was when what we understand by the " Harvest" meant no more to the average English- man than that which related to the in-gathering of British crops. But the time has long gone, and the latter-day Briton who thinks anything at all about the matter, is as much intereet..d in the yield of North American wheat fields as in that of the land Ithich comes up to his own door. This state of things, moreover, has become established and per- manent. The world's yield is the all-absorbing consideration, and the quantities of wheat grown in the various grain-pronucing and gran-exporting Countries is, indeed, remarkable. Failure in One region baa been compensated by enormous crops in other parts. Thus the North American continent, and the Dominion of Canada in particular, has found the present year to be one of great abun- dance; and inasmuch as North America has now become the "dominant partner" in the comity of corn-growing natione, the possiLility of a rise in price in England is remote. Consequently, also, as tar as the heads of numerous families are concerned the prospect of a bread famine in the winter is removed, together with the chances of the demon speculator. For North America alone is expected to yield little less than a hundred million quarters, a quantity approximating to one-third of the wheat harvest of the civilised world. The European crop is roughly estimated to yield 170 million quarters, which is fully ten million quarters less than the harvest of the last cereal year. The home crop may in the same way be taken to represent seven million quarters, arid, inasmuch as the whole king- dom consumes about thirty million quarters of whew., the other twenty-three million quarters will heve to be imported from abroad; which at least offers a good prospect for the Atlantic shipping trade in corn and flour.

There has been a good deal of discussion by mem- bers of local authorities in the provinces on the question whether measles should be included in the list of notifiable diseases, and, as might be expec- ted, the subject has now cropped up in the Metropolis. If the rredical officer of the newly con- stituted borough of Paddington could have his way, British housewives would be penalised for omitting to notify the fact when their children suffer from measles. In his annual report Dr Dudlield points out that measles is incontestably an infectious disease, that neglected patients are especially liable to lung disease, which too often leads to tuber- culosis, and be aids that in his opinion it is the duty of the Legislature to authorise the imposition of penalties in the We eits of the public generally, and families in particular.

A propos it may be mentioned that the Keynsham Rurai District Council tbe other day, by special resolution. recognised the skill and energy of its medical officer, Dr Heaven, in having combatted and checked a sharp outbreak of diphtheria at Brislington, near Bristol, of such a character that it was considered the public might well join in the congratulations officially. Dr Heaven has paid much attention to the subject, and had no hesita- tion in determining what course to take when the outbreak occurred. He acted promptly, on the lines suggested by modern observation, and success happily attended his efforts. It has been observed that diphtheria is a particularly difficult disease over which to exercise effective contrel, because it often occurs in a form whici easily ecapes ee-ec- tion, while it may he productive in ()niers ot the most dangerous symptoms.

Letters which have one after another appeared in a London paper have led to the inquiry whether we are on the eve of another development in teletr- r3phy, and to the expression of a hope that it may prove to b 3 so. Fir3t, a correspondent mentioned that anyone standing outside a provincial post office (Sxet er) could hear the instruments at work, and that, if acquainted with the system, he could not fall to understand what messages were passing. Then another writer tells how, when gning over the General Post Office, he found one "unattended instrument" working vigorously. Asking for the cause,he was infer Led that alio:less- ages went through these instrumette,and afterlisten ing a few minutes,his guide was able to tell him that at that time the War Office weLe communicating with the gunpowder works at Waltham Abbey. Now, if one of the results of the present system under which the instruments are rend by sound and not by sight. is that anybody with hearing keen enough and a knowledge of the code, can understand the messages being received at the post offices, where the sound of the instruments can be beard outside;it is plain that the sooner we go back to the sight-reading method the better. But is there I not a Marconi or other telegraphic expert who can help the public in this matter ?

When cyclone and anti-cyclone mset,then camas the tug of war--and a deluge! The rainfall in lees than twenty-four hours, reckoned from noon on Sunday made up and exceeded the ordinary August average in some parts of the country. and since then, the disturbance has been general, with the result that many have been sadly inconvenienced, or worse, while some have been greatly rejoiced. Among the latter the British farmer with his root crops looms largely, and included in the former were many thousands of seaside and other holiday ' makers. The drop in the thermometer on Monday and Tuesday was very remarkable, and the casual- ties along the coast have since furnished much un- ! pleasant reading.

SERVICES IN HILL CLIFFE GRAYEYARD.—These services were continued last Sunday night, when a fairly good congregation Resembled, notwithstanding the threatened storm. The service had not been held on the previous Sunday night owing to the absence of the pastor. Mr Hughes preached on " The ministry of our shadows," Acts V. 15th verse, dealing with out personal influence. There was good singing, led by a full choir. The last of these services for the season will be held to-morrow night to commence at 6.15.

WIDNES PAINTER SENT TO PRISON FOR EMBEZZLEMENT.

At Liverpool, last Friday before Mr W J Stewart stipendiary, William Owen, 31, variously described as a painter and a traveller. of 12 Thorpe-street, Widnes, was charged with embezzling several slims of money belonging to the Stan- ley Paint Manufacturing Company, by whom he was engaged as a traveller. The prisoner pleaded guilty to the charge. Tha total defalcations amounted to about £3B 10s. Prisoner was arrested by Detective-Sergeant Lind- say, and Mr Robinson informed his worship that Owen had been previously convicted of forgery at Mold Assizes, where he was sentenced to six months' imprisonment. He was now sent to gaol for three months with hard labour.

[BY A CO]RESPONMINT].

am able to give some further news of the Trans- porter Bridge this week, and ie state that work will be coinmenced definitely in September. It would have commenc-qt earlier but for a slight oversight on the part of those responsible for " the Drafting et the Bill," inasmuch as no arrangement was made with the Ship Canal Company and the Upper Mersey Navigation Trustees to cover the in- terruptions to traffic during construction. The matter has now been rectified and the contracts are laid with capable firms,; but I leave the rest to the next monthly meeting of the Urban Council, when, in all probability, the town's direetor will tell us all we desire to know.

Thanks to the exertions of Mr Byfield, Thomas- street, Runcorn, the town is now providel with a set of grapples of its own. lhey are gruesmie, but, under existing circumstances, necessary arti- cles. The set is complete and lengthy enough to drag the Ship Canal,and also contains one specially designed by Captain Waring for use in the Docks. The pity of the whole thing is that drags are neces- sary at all. What I should like to see would be proper steps taken to prevent there ever beirg a need for grapples.

The Runcorn Brewster Sessions give us food for reflection, and reflection of a kind which no Tee- ponsible townsman will shirk. Superintendent Ennion's statistics work out to a licenoe for every 206 of:the population. On the showing of one of the applicants for a new licence, it was stated that in the .11eath Ward there was a mpulation of some 2,300 and only one " public-house " therein. The Bench seemed fully convinced too, that the district did not require any more drinkingfacilities. Surely then, if that is the proportion they feel justified in maintaining, it is clear there must be too many licences in some localities, In face of this one would ask what is the duty of the Licensing BAnch ? Chralv, they should no longer allow us to suffer for the sins of our fathers (who granted the licences) but by a vigorous action they thould commence to let the licensed victualler know he is a pablic set- I vent, with a privileged duty to discharge for the public, and not the possessor of a monopoly, the letters patent of which are as unalterable as the laws of the Medes and Persians.

The reading public of Runcorn are requested to pay attention tl a notice itsued by the Runcorn Free Library Committee, which, is to the effect that the lending library is open from 8 p m. to 8 p.m. on Friday evenings instead of Wednesdays. Oiher evenings the library is open at the usual hours The change is made to meet the public needs.

Runcorn Wesleyan Methodists mar rejoice with heartfelt rejoicing, for their work (in so far as the circuit scheme is concerned) is not yet ended. Methodists—especially those of the Wesleyan per- suasion—are never happy unless they have some task to perform; and one of the greatest preachers of the day has said "That a chapel with a deist is a good thing for the flock," his obvious meaning being it keeps them busy. Hence the Methodists of the Runcorn Wesleyan Circuit may rejoice, inas- much as more work has been found for them not withstanding all they have accomplished sad their efforts in the future are to be exp Ended on the erection of a third minister's house, and extension work at Halton. The enterprise is one worthy of their finest traditions, and they have with such leaders as they possess every prospect of success.

The interesting square of glass spoken about by Mr John Frodsham,as beaeng the name of Mr John Wesley, should, if possible, be sought out; and if not kept among the treasures of the Runcorn Wesleyan Circuit, a place might be found for it in the archives of the Runcorn Free Library. Its historical value to the district is invaluable, and I do hove someone will interest himself in the matter. Mr W Handley or Mr F Hutton might set out on its track, and see what can be accomplished.

The fortnightly meeting of the above body was held at the Workhouse, Dutton, on Tuesday, when there were present:—Mr J Knowles, J.P, presiding, Admiral Joaes Parry, Messrs J Mclntyre, J Moseley Williams, Thomas Wright, A 0 Guest, T Baxter, 0 E Linaker, H Talbot, P Gleave, C Roylance, J Mounfield, G Pilling, Lewis, B Mawdaley, T Darlington, E Clarke, J Bolehaw, W H Bradford, E Bretherton, Jos Baguley, A Eaton, with Mr Geo F Ashton (clerk), Mr W E Hough (assis- tant clerk), Mr Jno Farrington (inspector), Messrs Diggle and Swinton (surveyors), and Dr Adams (medi- cal officer).
THE THELWALL NUISANCE. FURTHER CORRESPONDENCE.

The following letters were read by the Clerk : " Easton Tower near Tarporley, Cheshire, August 22ad 1901. To Geo. F. Ashton Eeq., Runcorn Rural Dig trict Council. Dear Sir: In the press report of the last meeting of the Runcorn Rural Distriet Council I notice my name was mentioned by Admiral Jones-Parry in connection with the nuisance arising from the Grappen- hall Tanneries. I resided in the immediate neighbour- hood of these tanneries for many years and can safely say that the smell arising theretrorn was not objectionable in any way but rather the reverse and at a later period, when the rebuildiug of my brother's house necessitated my continuous residence there I cannot remember any- thing beyond the ordinary smell of a tanyard. Duringl the course of our operations it became necessary to cover the brook which forms the boundary between the townships of Grappenhali and Thelwall and which runs between my brother's property and the tanneries and I arranged an interview with Mr Malnryre, who is a member of your Board and the agent of the owner of the tanneries, and he met Mr Long and myself on the scot and arranged a give and take line so as to straighten the boundary and admit of the introduction of earthenware pipe; with which we had decided to cover the brook in place of the ordinary brick culvert. As a quantity of water passes dawn during heavy raise it was necessary to have a pipe of the largest size. The work was carried out by Mr Elwin Wood, of Widnes, who is a professional con- tractor, and my brother's drains were connected on the newest principle then adopted. A very much smaller pipe of course sufficed to conve) the sewage water to the brook, and I menet understand your Medical Officer describing the brook as a two feet sewer, but possibly he means the stream proceeding from the tanneries,and which joins the brook lower down the stream. A few years afterwards the smell from the tanneries bscame very obnoxious, owing, as I have been inforrhed, to some new system of tanning being adopted there, Xand there was quite an epidemic of diphtheria—a disease of which I cannot remember a single case in the neigh- bourhood. I must say I could hardly believe the smell was so bad as represeoted, and I rather ridiculed the matter, but after a recent experience,to which Admiral Jones-Parry referred, I am convinced that there is some poisonous smell or gas proceeding from the tanneries. I had been os cling in the country and on my way back to Warrington was pasting the tanneries at about midnight when I unfortunately inhaled some. thing of tire vilest description which made me feel as if I wanted to throw up the whole of my supper at oncP.l was quite ill from the effects for several days. The wind was blowing from the direction of the tanneries at the time, and across the highway which passes immediately in front. What it was I got a breath of I do not know, but I have not been that way since as J should not care to have a further similar experience. It might be some kind of gas that is discharged during the night, but it must be of a very injurious nature. I do not go so far as to say that the epidemic of diphtheria was causecTby the smell, but this disease has certainly made its appearance in the immediate neighbourhood since the new system of tanning, if such it be, has been introduced, and I think the public ought to know what that system is as they could perhaps then be able to judge for themselves if ' your doctors continue to disagree but no Icroubt you have good reasons for holding back that portion of your expert's report dealing with thia disagreeable subject. One of your members, at a recent meeting of your board mentioned the case of a passing cyclist who had been similarly affected by the smell, so that there mutt be other sufferers than myself, and should perhaps be in order if as one of the representa tives of the Cyclists' Tourine Club, I took the opportu nity of asking your board to protect) ;your cycling con- stituents from being partially poisoned with these noxious vapours while engaged in what ought to be an enj yable and healthy pastime. Roping that the lm nodule. of the subject may be considered as an ample apology for the length of this letter, yours truly, John Naylor. Gentlemen, as Mr Ashton told me to send on the letter I had written to him, I think it is only justice that I should write to tell you of the vile smells we have had to endure this last week only. chiefly during the night time. Monday nieht at 11.30, a keen acrid stench filled our house and kept us awake until 3 a.m., Tuesday,when the vile stench abated. Again on 'rues- day midnight a very keen acrid stench came hot and scourging through the crevices of the window frames, it awoke me it was so strong, and by one o'clock everyone of us were awakened by the same cause, and all were affected in the same way, the vileness of the stench caused us all to have diereses)", until 5 a.m. Wednesday when the stench abated. Tnis in a civilized country allowed to be continued because the tanyard is worked by men of means, otherwise I expect they would be forced to Lbate such nuisance on tne same lines as the case (in the" Guardian" August 3rd) where a man was summoned for keeping two pigs which caused a nuitance that Dr Adams condemned as being a nuisance injurious to health, Mr Farrington being witness in the case. Yet Dr Adams declares this tanyard is not injur- ious to health although no 200 pigs, ' nor pig testes, mould cause the stench it does. As regards I the Medical °Ric, eta statement about the Tanyard men I suppose he got his information from thee 'petition which was signed on blank sheets of paper and the words written afterwardg,some of the men not even hearing what the petition was. The first death which occurred was a little child on the Tannery premises, which I heard was from a poisoned throat. Whet we want isa little more truth, this horrid nuisance stating I and the tannery carriedeen on the usual system Supposing to oblige yoar council we say the tanyard men do not smell the odours, yet you might as well say because I slaughter house men do not suffer other people cannot. !Plenty of 'people here if you will send your expert, Dr. Penny over again will testify to ' him that his report is not COO stroog seeing what they have suffered. Dr. Penny saw the cesspool with 6in. of foam. Last year we took samples for your Medical Officer when the foam was 41t. 2iu. thick, so as hat would Dr Penoy have thought of that ? The whole tannery gives out vile stench; not just the brook, the are properly settling tanks especially,which you 1345, csnstructed. They are not constructed at all, being only holes duglin toe ground without any sides or bottoms. We want to know whether Mr Long or your Council is going to compensate us and others for all we have lost ; and as this tanyard has cost us alone £5O, which means nearly all our savings, you will see now we are placed. We should be glad if your Council will tell us this and oblige, yours respectfully, L. LEAH, August 24th, 1901." 'the Clerk : Tnis is the whole of tne correspoodenco I have, but there ie the report of the committee app emot- ed to visit the place and see Mr Long. Mr Pilling stated that the committee had really nothing to report, only to say they were no further than they were before. Mr Long very strongly objected to the brook being piped over in any way. The Chsirtnan : Did he give any reason ?

Mr. Pilling t Hi 4 reason appeare Ito be he wag ps.r- fectly satisfied that what went down the brook was perfectly clear ; and not only that, bat that it tended to cleanse the brook of sewage. Mr Mclntyre added a further reason, that if the brook was piped over all sorts of filth might descend without being seen, and deposit on Mr Loog's land on the other side of the canal. _
The Coairman observed at a later state they did not Seem to be any further advanced from their point of view.

_ Then the discussion was raked up from the very com- moncement and the old ground travelled over to no purpoie. Dr Adams was hevd to say that if tie Tannery was not there and the diluent was not there, the nuisance would be there. Mr Talbot pointed out this Fignifi.d they could leave the Tanyard out of the reckoning. The doctor had been 18 months on the work. Would he tell them where the nuisance did come fram. Dr Adams then stated that he said at much greater length than he now put it :—" That the two sewers in conjunctiOn form the nuisance." The sewer from Waste-lane and the sewer from Mr Naylor's. At the present time, however, Mr Naylor was pumping his sewage over his land, by means of a tank and hand pump. After wasting considerably over an hour in trying to find a remedy for the evil, End suggestmg that the Council should cleanse their own sewer, it was decided on the motion of Mr S Woodward that a committee should be appointed to consider a siwerage scheme for Thelwall. The following were elected on the committee —Messrs J Mclntyre, G Filling, 8 Woodward, .1. MOUII. field, Bradford. Talbot, and the Chairman ; the Medical Officer, Inspector and Surveyors were also instructed to attend the committee meeting.

div.head: INQUESTS AT RUNCORN.
div.p: INQUESTS AT RUNCORN.
More Drowning Cases.

On Saturday afternoon Mr R Dobson, ceronor,beld an inquest at Runcorn Police Court, tchiching the death of George Edward Spencer, infant son of Edward Spencer, who wadi found drowned in the Bridgewater Canal on Friday morning.—Edith Spencer, wife of Edward Spencer, waterrnan, 36, Canal-street, Runcorn, identi- fied the body as that of her son. There was no gate to the yard, and there had been none while she had lived there. The boy went out at the front door in Canal- street.—A juror : To get on the canal bank be would have to go about 20 yards.—The Coroner : I think it would be some protection for little children if a gate were provided for the Lack yard. The jury returned a verdict of "Found drowned." On Tuesday afternoon Mr R Dobson, coroner held another inquest at the Runcorn police court on the body of Alfred Fishwick aeed 8 years, of 3, Back-Penketh- lane, who was drowned on Sunday evening.—John Fishwick, labourer, identified the body as that of his son. He last saw him on the canal bank at the top of Ashridge-street on Sunday afternoon. They did not , become uneasy about him until 7.30 p.m. as he had several aunts he visited. Runcorn and Halton were searched witheut result and information was given t-. 1 the police. Mr Byfield recovered the boy's body from the Bridgewater Canal near the Sprinch at 6 a.m. on Monday.—John Harper Fishwick aged 13, brother of the deceneed, deposed to seeing the deceased on the canal bank between three and four on Sunday after- noon. He was close to the crane at the " bau ks." He had a piece of string tied to the crane and he had the other end in the canal. He (witness) did not know what he was 'doing : he bad no hooks to the string.— Mr By field deposed to grappling for the boy tor an hour on Sunday night, but did not find him. At sia o'clock on Monday inorning he Slaw a piece of string in the water and he found that deceased was entangled with the string and he pulled him to the surface. A verdict of "Found drowned" was returned. Mr Raining aNked theCotoner to express the thanks of of the jury to Mr /Wield for the eervicei he rendered now and then in cases of this kind.

The Coroner said he very much appreciated all Mr By- field bad done not enly in this case but in many others. Mr Byfieldrhad been instrumental in procuring drags that were kept at the Police Station and were easily accessible He bad always found Mr Eyrield ready and willinz to help anyme in trouble and he dii not think thee cluid say too ranch in.. commendation of Mr Bvfield's eff )rta.
Mr Byfield repliel that it was very pie.asing to hear these r:nnarks. Be wallcl always be willing to d 3 all he could as long as he lived.

div.head: REMARKABLY SUDDEN DEATH.
div.p: A REMARKABLY SUDDEN DEATH.

Mr R Dotson, c moner, held an inqaes; at Runcorn on Tuesday afternoon on the body of Peter Brown, aged 48 years, ot 10, Spring-street, who died very suddenly on Monday morning. Loaisa Brown, widow of the deceased, deposed that he was captain of a flat and he left home on Monday morning about 8.15 to go by train to Manchester where his flat was lying. He was apparently in good health. Hs had not complained of being unwell; An hour later he was brought tonne and said he Was 111, and wanted to go to bed. He was put to bed and the doctor sent for. When D: Robinson arrived shanty afterwards he Was dead.

Dr Bethune, who had made •a post-mg/leo/. examina- tion, said the cause of death waa kearc failure, due to fatty degen-ration of the heart. This was hastened by the man g)ing enut mufflrinl frxn pl•urn Doournonia. A verdict in accordance wit `i the medical te3tirnony was returned.

Present: Messrs S Pope (chairman), W Handley, W Hankinson, F W Button, T Riley, D Bisbrown, and J F Moulton, and Mrs Jones (librarian). . IRE ANNUAL REPORT AND FINANCIAL STATEMENT. ' The financial statement for the year ended March 31st r 1901. showed receipts as follows :—Balance at cons- mencsrnent of year, £l7 16s 21; fines £7 64 8 1 ; borrowers' ticket., £5 119 El ; catalogues, £3 193 21 ; Isafes of papers, £2 123 31; sub.cri ' p-ions £1 4s ; dons- th m us, £5 . from library rate, £124 ; balance in hand, I£B 43 41. The Librarian alio submitted the report on the year's work of the Library. During 1980-1901, The total issues from tie lending department were 22,150, made up as f :Bows :—Tbeology 285, philosophy and political e;:momy 157, science and art 786. history., biography, and travel 898, poe:try and the drama 83, 1 prose fiction 18.156 miscellaneous literature, 1,630, Freon literature 18, music 137. The number of borrowers' ticketa issued during the year ended June 30th, 1901, aas 673, viz, 343 males, and 330 females. The increase on last year was 13. The number of , subscribing members being non-residents was 21, toe same as last _rear. The total number of volumes in the

library was 11,536. The classification of the work 4in the lending library was as follows :—Theology 578, nbiloslpby and pobtical economv 247. science and art 955, history, blozrap`ly and travel 232. prose ficion 4,423, miscellaneous literature 58, music 210 Oa the motion of Mr Bisbrown, seconded by Mr Riley, the report was adopted. "A RECORD OF THE LATE LIBRARIAN."

The Chairman sail it had been suggested that there should be some reference to the services of their late librarian in the annual report. (Hear, hear.) They asked Mr Handley if he would be good enough to pre- pare an obitnary notice, as he had known the late Mr ty D Jones in connection with the library from the begin- ning. Indeed, Mr Handley knew probably more of the library movement in Runcorn than any man living. Ur Handley complied with the request, and he submitted the following for their acceptsucei—"lt is with feelings of sincere regret that the Library Committee places on record the decease of its esteemed librarian. From the inceotion of the free library movement, in the year 1879, Mr Rises, with the characteristic impulsiveness of his ardent nature, by voice and pen, took a prominent part in its advocacy, little dreaming that he was thus unconsciously proving his especial fitness for the official . duties he was as sequently called upon to undertake. In its development. Tue Free Libraries Acts were adopted at a public meeting of ratepayers on the 19th December ! 1881, and almost immediately afterwards Mr Jones was I unanimously appointed by the Free Library Committee its firss librarian. Tale appointment was no sinecure, involving not only the classification, cataloguing, and arrangement of the comparatively small number of volumes which were the nucleus of the Free Library. bet also the creation and fostering of an in- stitution demanding a wide acquaintance with general literature, and a rare discrimination in the selection and suggestion of books Suitable for a public library, and also keeping abreast of the stream constantly iasuiryg from the public press. No the least important service I rendered by Mr Jones was his readiness in assisting I readers in the choice of books, his judgment and advice ! doubtless being aided by his personal acquaintance with the tastes, needs, and environment of those seeking his ; guidance. Never was a committee more fortunate in its choice, or a publio more faithfully or loyally served. His literary sympathies, his knowledge of books, his retentive memory, and his natural aptitude won and retained the confidence and es'eem of all. For wed nigh ?J.) year; the library was his care, its welfare his first and last thought, and his enduring memorial is the noble institution to which. he so lovingly devoted the best y ears of his life." The Chairman moved that this notice be printed in the annual report. Mr Hankinson seconded,and remarked that tbe notice was to the point, and embodied all that was required. He thought they were indebted to Mr Handley for its precaration. _ _ _
Mr 13 shrown elpported, and the motion was carried.
