FOR PRESTON BROOK.
Opening Ceremony.

In connection with the Runcorn Wesleyan circuit extension scheme, a most interesting afternoon and evening were spent on Wednesday last, at Preston , Brook, when the ceremony of opening the new Sunday School there, was performed by Mr R U Posnett. 1 History undoubtedly places Preston Brook amongst the oldest of the centres of Wesleyan Methodism, for not only have the greatest preachers of the Methodist church preached therein, but John Wesley himself has filled its pulpit and left a trace of his great influence behind.

On Wednesday afternoon, the Runcorn Friends, gathered in goodly number at Top Locks, where a com- modious covered barge was boarded and a delightful sail by way of the Bridgewater Canal, landed the party an hour later, atiPreston Brook village. The walk up to the Chapel was soon accomplished,and uniting with the Preston Brook frieuds ia front of athe new schools, the whole party burst forth into song, and the strains of the charming hymn " Corns let us join our cheerful voice" rose in thankfulness to God at the consua:mation of a lorg felt desire. . . .

The R.";‘, J B Poster then led in prayer after wbich The Rev H Morrison cslled up3u Ntr K a Poitiett to open the new ibuilding iu place of Mrs Posnett, whom all regretted was unable to attend. Mr Posnett then turned the key and led the way into the new building.

Th:r new structure, is 'situate on land adjoining the chapel, the site having been presented to the Trustees by Sir Gilbert Green&ll, It has a lean-to roof lighted by three ski- ights, and is most commodious and admir- ably suited for the purposes of a Sunday school. There is a large window at one end, and two windows in the side wall of the Chapel receive light tor that p!a2o from the roof of the new wing. The schoolroom has three entrances, and a small class-room and when it is con- sidered that at present the school roll nusioloors but some 60 scholars, it is quite evident that tbe building will meet the needs of the village for many years to come. ' On the people assembling inside, Mr Posnett said be wished to utter one word sif apology on behalf of bis wife waom he was sorry to say was unable to be pre- sent, If she could have seen her way to come she would have come,—(hear hear)—and the last words she said to him were . I hope you will do it well as you are doieg it on my behalf. (pause.) She wished well o God's service in the district, and espfcially to Preston Brook, which was the place where so many of their local preachers made their first efforts. (Hoar, bear). 01 her behalf he had great pleasure in declaring the School- room opened. At the earns time he must say how Mrs Posnett hoped, and how they all hoped, for the glory of God, and for the love of little chddren that building might be put to its noblest and highest use. (Loud applause). Mr S Taylor then stepped forward and presented Mr Festoon, on behalf of his wife with a handsome copy of " John Wesley; his own biographer." The presenta- tion, he explained was made on behalf of the Trustees as a memento of the occasion. The book bore the inscription, " Presented to Mrs R H Posnett on the occa- sion of opming the New Sunday School, at Preston Brook, August 28th, 1901." Mr Posnett briefly acknowledged the gift, and that portion of the ceremony ended in the singing of the Doxology.

div.head: SERVICE II THE CHAPEL. __ . _
div.p: SERVICE II THE CHAPEL. __ . _

The Rev T J Caoate (Chairman of the Liverpool Districr), then officiated at a well attended service, held in the Cove!, and preached a powerful discourse from 2 Kings, 6:h chapter, 15. ti verse. He illustrated man's dependency upon God, the influence of Wesleyanism upon the morals of the world arid the 101 l aence playesl by so called insignificant and obscure personages in all paths of life, finally bringing his disicourse to bear upon toe importance of the undertaging. the completion of which they celebrated that day._

div.head: AFTERNOON TEA.
div.p: AFTERNOON TEA.

By the time the service was over, tea had be laid in the schoolroom, and was admirably served to all by the following ladies :—Mrs Jones, Miss Sr*, Miss Jones, Miss Nellie Grounds,Mrs Grounds, Miss Grounds, Miss Rossbottom, Mrs S2ragg, Mrs James Webo, Miss Louie Webb, Mns R Webb, Miss Sissie Grounds, Mrs Alfred Jones, Mrs Prince, Mrs R -Meets, Mrs John Webb, Miss Lena Webb, Mrs Putts,and Miss Berta Webb (the chapel organist),

div.head: EVENING MEETING.
div.p: THE EVENING MEETING.

Teo evening meeting was held in the chapel end was presided over by Mr John Frodsham (a former superin- tendent of Preston Broom Soinday School). Torre were also present :—The Revs T J Choate (Liverpool), A Wells (itiperintendent),H Morrison, J B Foster, W Acre (Runcorn), Messrs R El Fosnett. F J Norman. S Taylor, J 111 Fein, P James Webb, S Coventry, Captain W Millington, E Una worth, George Hayes. T Leach, R ' Rawlinson. James Greenalgn, A Riley, J W Temperley, and an influential gathering of ladies The Cnairman, having expressed the very great pletsure it gave him to be preseet, lamented the fact that there were not now many of the old faces he loved to see in the oays of his happy congestion with that olace left for them t) gaz i on, Still he was deliehted 0 recognise many of the younger ones which had grown in their place. (Hear, bear.) The historical associations ef Preston Brook were taro ot interest, for John Wesley preached there ie 17E5 or 1766, whilst at Preston Brook he was also said coI have inscrib-d his earns on a square of glass. Be did not know whether Mr Wells (their present superin- tendent) had it, but the last time he saw it was in Mr Wells study. Mr Bradley load it then. Underneath J)lin Wesley'a name there was ineribed the name of one of his colleagues, so that the " square" was ample corroooration of the fact that John Wesley had preached there. (Anplause). Mr Frodeuam then sketched the history of the chapel and school from their foundetiou in IEI9 and IE2O respectively, told of how they originally belonged to the Warrington circeit, of the strike of the Warrington local preachers ; and Pres- ton Brook's subsequent attachment to the Runcorn , Circuit, subsequent to the payment of the debt on the I ehapol by Mr Teffer. In concluding Mr Frodsham also rreferred to the usefulness of Sunday School work and said that itshould be a nursery for the Methodist chapels Methodism was a thing to be proud of—(hear,hear,)— and they should so live and work that the benefits of ' Methodism might be conferred upon their fellow , creatures. (Applause). He lamented the loss Preston Brook Chapel had sustained through the death of the late Mr Johnson, but though he was gone from their midst it still remained for them so to live that they might meet him in Heaven. (App'ause.) Mr F J Norman who described himself as the "general 'knockabout" of the Runcorn Circuit—(laughter)--spoke I with deep regret of toe absence of Mr J R Frith • Mr S Taylor whom they:had almost to worm not of his corner with a screw jack, and his fellow treasurer always seemed to leave time talking to him. (Laughter.) Re therefore had a sort of double barrelled purpose to fulfil and he would refer to the Runcorn Circuit scheme, not so much for the in formation of those present, as for the inform- ation of their District Chairman. (Hear, hear.) . It was not often they had the Chairman of the District amongst them, and it would not be Very long before , that gentleman would be called upon to take a hand in the Division of ttes Million Guinea Fend. (Applause.) It wasithe'wisdom and foresight of their superintendent (Mr Welts) that had brought Mr Choste amongst them, SO that he might See what they had done for themselv:s in the Runcorn Circuit, and as their superintendent he would be in abetter position to secure to them a "large slice " of the million. (Laughter and Applause.) Mr Norman then illustrated bow the need of Sclioo!s at Weston Point had been the primary factors in bringing about the Circuit scheme which had resulted in good work being done at Bruns- wick, Halton-toad, Weston Point, and Preston Brook ; hut impressed upon his hearers that the scheme was not to be complete with the conclusion of that work. (Hear, hoar.) There was Halton and Mr S Barrow to be considered—(laughter,)—and no scheme for the circuit would be complete without considering Halton. (Ariplaulee.) And finally it was th,ir intention of pro- viding a third minister's house. (Loud applause.) Some people eould ask why these things had not been men- tioned at the outset. Well, he was of opinion it was not always wise to commence with too great a loarelt wan al- ways best to keep a little in hand. (Hear, hear.)ln Con- cluding. Mr Norman spoke of the magnificent antidote to sacerdotalisre the system of local preachers as main- tained by the Wesleyan body proved both in the town and vi lige, and prayed to God that the work at Preston Brook would be as beneficial in the future as it had been in the pest. (Loud applause). Mr II H Posrett next delivered an address: After alluding to several refreshing reminise eoces, he said he had ta thank God for the many privileg,s which had come into his life through his association with Method- ism. Mr Posnett then referred to his visit to the Con- ference, and spoke of the vast amount of knowledge he , had gained by the visit. He was astonished when he ' heard the amount of money which the ruple called Methodists were giving on behalf of the Chapel building up and down the country. One speaker, be believed it was Dr Waller announced from the platferm that at that moment there was being spent in chapels in course of erection three quarters of a million, and he said that amount could have been set out at almost any moment during the last two or three years. Their chapel building should be in exact proportion to the love they had for Christ, and the love they had for ' Christ's church. In conclusion he said he felt grateful to Mr Choate for coming there and showing his sym- paths, with them in their efforts, to do something for Methodism in their circuit. They wished to help them- selves, and to induce him to help them. (Applause.) The Rev T J Choate, in a lengthy address dealt with the vastneas of the chapel building schemes throughout the connexion, giving the amount expended on such projects, and said he rejoiced in that evidence that the church to which they belonged was a living, vigorous, active church, and that those immense sums of money had not been the gifts of wealthy people who could spare the contributione. There were very few wealthy people in Methodism. It was a mistake to characterize the Methodist Church as wealthy. They had a very large

company of people like some they had in the Runcorn circuit, that were comfortable. He did not think that any church in the world possessed such • community of generous poor folk than the Methodist Church.(Hear, hear). The people who had given the million guineas to the Century fund were people whose gifts bad been most selbsacrificing—the poor folks. If the small pro- portion of rich folk had given anything like in propor- tion to the labouring men they would have had a good deal more than the one million guineas. He was very glad they were doing something in that village for the religious instruction of (he children. The rev gentle- man then spoke at length regarding the great responsi- bility of training the children. He was thankful for the good work done in the circuit, and he was sure a con- tinuance of work in the same spirit would be blessed, and God would render their labours prosperous. He promised to do whatever he could for Runcorn with regard to the million fund. (Applause). The Rev A Wells said they mtiq express their great admiration for the beautiful spirit that had been shown I by the people of Presto!' Brook themselves in the matter (Hear, hear.) He was very thankful that a real spirit of devotion and progress was being manifested in that ' place. They bad sent nearly £lOO from that place towards the fund and he thought they were justified in offering to them their congratulations, and at the same time expressing their determinati n to see them through in that matter,and help them more readily because they had made Frith a beautiful attempt to help themselves. Mr J M Frith proposed a vote of thanks to the Chair- man and Mr Choate, and spoke ot the improvements that had been effected.

Mr Taylor seconclod. After alluding to the circuit scheme, he observed that they did not mean to let things rest until Haltou had been helped in some material manner. He lived their frienCs who were distributing the million funds would not lose sight of them. (Applause), The motion was unanimously carried, and the meeting closed with the Dmtology.

div.head: COST OF PAFPERISIS.
div.p: COST OF PAFPERISIS.

Mr. Dansey's statement of pauperism and expenditure in the counties of Chester, Derby, Hereford, Salop, Stafford, and Worcester was submitted. It showed that the cost per head on the population for the Runcorn Union was ls 3i, whilst the charge for the other Unions in the County of Cheshire was as follows:—Birkenhead., Is Thi; Bucklow, 1114 ; Chester, 24 4i; Congleton, is 5i ; Ma:icleefield, is 71 I ; Nantwicn, Is 9d; Northavich, is 311 ; Stockport, is 511 ; Tarvin, Is 2td; Wirral, Is 11 The total number ot paupers relieveu in the Runcorn Union up to January Ist 1901; was 564, as compared with 586 up to January Ist 1933, and 1106 to the same date it 1E72. The expenditure for ths half year ended Lady Day, 1901 was £2,674, as contrasted wit'l £2,403 for half-year ended 1900,and £2,792 for half year ended Lady Day 1872. This represented an increase for half-year ended Lady Day 1901, as compared with that of 1900, of £271. The Clerk in submitting the report of Mr Danes,. pointed out that the cost in the Runcorn Union was 311 less than the average for the District, covered by tue report. This was considered satisfactory. THE VACCINATIOrI FEES.

Mr Mclntyre reported that the Committee appointed to consider the question of the Vaccination Fees had met that morning. but as they were already paying on the lowest possible scale they did not think aavthing could be done to effect a reduction. It was decided, however. to kepp a watchful eve on leßistation, and to join any association of Hoards of Guardians likely to have in view aRy scheme of improvement. The report was adopted. div.p: THE 330175 E COMMITTEE.

Mr Moseley Williams submitted the revrt of the House Committee,which showed there were 137 inmates as against 122 for the corresponding period of last year in the house. A slight alteration was proposed in the dietary of the officers,and it was recommendel that the children should have a day in Delamere Forest instead of • day at the seaside. Before the report was:adopted, it was known that the trip to the seaside was provided by subscription, and not out of the rates and that the trip to Delamere Forest would bs met by the balance in band from he last trio fund.

Mr. Reynolds also explained that the children had been twice to the seae last rear, and Delamere Forest wag a recommendation of the Master's as a change. The House Committee had accepted the Master's suggestion unanimously.
The repori of the Howe Committee ;sac then adopted.

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES

THEFT FROM THE CEMETERY —A WARNING TO OTHERS.— NUMEROUS COMPLAINTS A girl nulled Betsy Mills, living at 23, Orford-s -reE t was brouetit beforu the magistrates at the Warrington Police Court on Monday, and charged with committing damage at the Cemetery by tak ng a piece of ribbon drom a hu.ch ot timers on July 31-rt.—Mr Stanley Wilson, Deputy Town Clerk, conducted the case on behalf of the Corporation and feted that at 5 p to. en Wednesd the 3let ult, the Cemetery Itgietrar was oa dote in the Cemetery when he saw the defendant go up to a grave, pick up a bunch of flawers, strip off the ribbon with which they were tied, throw the flowers down again and put the ribbon in her packet. During the last two years there had bePn a great many complaints to the Cemetery committee about these petty and contemptible thelte. With the %insistence of the Chief Constable the com- mittee had done all they could to suppress the nuisance and to bring the off- adore before the magistrates. As the derenJant was rather young, the cammittee felt that if the Bench would express their opinion as to the way in which future cffenders would be dealt w;th, j,istice would be met if the case was withdrawn.—The C'erk said the full penalty was £s.—The Chairman said the ft2nch would be dispesed to inflict the full pmaltv in the future if the circurtattancos of the caaes aarnitted of it.—Toe Coief Constable said the nuisance was be- coming so great that the committee had called his attention to it and persona who intended offending °lee: t • know that two constab'es were kept on duty at th Cemetery and they (the offenders) would preb- ahly fall into their hands. —After cautioning the defend- ant, the magistrates discharged her.

DISGRACEYUL A FFAIa r SILVER-STREET--.WOMAN VIOLENTLY ASSAULTED. At the Warrington Po COUV: On Monday,hefore Mr F Monks . and ether magistrates, Patrick Thynne, 5, Silver-street, was charge with committing an aggra- vated assault upon Mary Warburton at 10 o'clock on Saturday night—at the outset the Chief Constable said the case was not so s-rious as it was at first anticipated it would be. Under ennaiderablr; provocation the prisoner committed an essault upon the :c-Amplainant, viol had , *lived with him for twelve years, some witnesses said by hicklng and others by thumping her. Her condition was such that she was taken to the Infirmary almost in a state ef collapse and after her injuries bad been dressed, was allowed to go lime. 'Nat morning the woman said elle was mole ts b ame td,n the priioner, owing t 3 tor bad habite—Mary Warburton, the corn- plaitient,was then called and said:she had lived with the prisoner as hie wife for 12 years. At 2.30 on Saturday afternonn, prisoner gave tier ha. and she went out and spent the money. She came home drunk at nighl and a quarrel arose between her and the prisoner.—The Cnief C instable proceeded to reed the statement made by the complainant on Saturday night. In it she said that the prisoner p eked up a chair and struck her on the back with it, exclaiming that he would " swing for her." She fell down and whilst she was on the floor he seized her by tie hair of the head and kicked her repe4te lly.—Complain- ant now showed a rr3ng desire to tcreen the prisoner, and denied that her statement on Saturday was a corrr ct version of the affair. She said prisoner gave her a " shove" and she fell against the craele.—Catherine learns, 10 years of age. residing at 16, Silver-street, said, that she saw Warburton and the pritnagr in Silver-street on taturday night. She heaxd complainant siasut " Don't kill me Pat and I will go borne." Prisoner thereupon gave her three kicks one in the middle of the back and two about the legs. Warburton fell down and he kicked her again. The woman was taken to the Infirmary.— Cara Airlock, a girl living at 5, Silvot-square, Paid she saw prisoner bang the woman's head against the wall. She fell to the ground and he riz id her by the hair of the head and dragged her into a house. Song t'eard the prisoner say" I have had no meat for four days." He kicked the woman on the back and legs—lnspector Taylor sa'd he was called to Silver-atreer, and saw Warburton who complained to him of prisoner's con- duct. She appea,ed to be in great agony and said be bad just returned from the Infirmary. 11Pr condition was such that witr,ess tsnk her hack to the Infirmary in a cab, and her i juries were again attended to. He subsequently annrehendel the prisoner who in answer to the charge elid "I have nothing to say. It serves e right for being a fool." He was perfectly saber. The statement read be the Chief Constable was made to witness by Warburton and when he read it to her on Saturday night she said it was true.—The Chief Con. rable said the prisoner had been subjected to consider- able neglect, if not illtreatment by the woman. Ile was a respectable man, so far as the police knew, and had never been before the Court previously. He bore a good character in the army and had a discharge.—The Chairman said the Bench consi lerccl prdionat had suffered very great provoe )n ant coosql Oly tee could not, take as serious a view rf the case so then otherwise would have done. He would be fined 51.

THEFT BY WAS CARTERS —SMART PENALTY. At the Dareileury Petty Seasiriip. on Tu.sday bctore Mr W Le ig (presiding) and other magietrateS, term earters named Joseph Monks. Porter-street,Wari and Richard Brocklehurst, Fairclough's-avenue, War- rington, were aharged with strilire 120 IN of flour and 60 lbe of provender, value 175 63, the pronerty of their employers Messrs James FaircleurA arid Sons, Limited.—Mr Unsworth, solicitor. prosecated nn behalt ot tl-n firm and stated that the defendant a had been in the employ cf the company as carters for two and three years respectively. For trines time past the prosecutors had had • reason to suspect that their carters were in the habit of nilfering. In this particular instance, ow to theing pr-inipt action which was taken by Sergeant Carter of Baretrin, to whcm the prosecutors wished to convey their thanks, they weirs enabled to at once seize upon be E-dir which had been stolen on the previous day. It had been pilfered from about twenty sacks, a few pounds from each. and the defendants disposed of it by selling it to Mrs Eldtsbeth Mores. wife of a roadman, residing in Ituncorn-rad, Little Legit. He had not been able to ascertain the circumstances under which she purchased the four but at all events she paid only about a fourth of its rest value: She gave 41 for nbout 120 pounds, the market value of which would be about 144. With regard to the prerrender, a hae contaicio. 601b5 was bought by the son, Joseph Moores. for 2s 3i whith was rely a fraction of its real value. In cons( quence of in- formation obtained the firm sent one of their travellers to Sergeant Carter, and together they went to Moores' house. At first it was denied that there was any flour or provender in the house. but ultimately it was ad- mitted.lf it had not tYea for the fact that they required Lividenoe from thens,Mrs Moores and the son would have been prosecuted for receiving the goods, knowing them to hays been stolen. It was necessary in order to prove the case, that they should have their evidence and that was the reason no proceedings were taken. This was not the first case at the sort which had occurred and the firm wished him to press the case as an example to the other carters and their employees generally.—Elizibeth Mosses was then called and stated that on Tuesday the :Oth !est the defendants came to the house and offered

) sell some flour. Her eon answered the door and witness said she did not want stay lour. She ultim- I ately told her son to give them 4s for it, and the .our wag left at the house. She did not know anything about the provender.—P.S. Carter spoke to going to the heuse and finding the flour and provender Mrs Moores said her son had bought it from Messrs Fairclough's carters. She admitted having paid 5s for a bag of flour three weeks ago.—Mr Unsworth pointed , out that by these thefts not only the firm but the [customers were robbed—. After consultation, the Chair- man said the employers must be protected against such systemized thieving. They were sorry to have to make ' an example of the defendants and hoped it would be a lesson to them. They imposed • fine of £3 aid costs wit° the alternative uf two months' imprisonment.— Mrs Moores and her son were brought forward and ceesured by the Bench for their part in the transaction. A RENT COLLECTOR'S RECEPTION—ASsAI7LTS BT A SANKEY BRIMS MAN—CONSTABLE LOSES BIS TEMPER. At the County Borough Police Court on Wednesday, before Mr T Birchall and other magistrates, William Cotton, 28, Plumpten-street, Sankey Bridges, was charged with assaulting Thomas Kilshaw, Police Constable Woods and Thomas Hough too pre- vious morning—Thomas Rilshaw, a rent col- lect m in the employ of T and J L Tunstall, Be weey Chambers, stated that at 10 o'clock the previous morning he was collecting rents in Plumpton-street and knocked at the door of number £B, where Cotton reside!. Receiving no answer he went to the beck door and saw Cotton. When witness told him he had called for the rent, prisoner struck him in the face with his fist. He want away from the door and prisoner followed him. They commenced wrest- ling together and prisoner said that if he got witness on the floor he would murder him. Witness managed to maintain the upper hand until P.C. Woods came upon the FCPV. Prisoner rushed at the constable and struck him. Oa being taken into custody he became very violent and kicked the officer; Thomas Hough, a watchman in the employ of Mes.rs Monks, Hall and Co., came to toe coostable's assistance, and he also was assaulted by the prisoner, who kicked him in the eye. Prisoner had to be handcuffed with his hands behind his back.—P.C. Woods stated that when he came upon the scene prisoner" ran at him with his head," but witncss stepped on one side, and prisoner's held came into cont let, with a wall,inflict- ing several injuries. Prisoner became like a madman,and kicked and tried to bite witness. Eventually he was obliged to handcuff him, and Thomas Hough came to his assistance and he was assaulted by the prisoner. As they were going along Sankey-street, prisoner threatened to kick some windows in, and they had to drag him along the middle of the road.—ln answer to the Cbief Constable witness said he adminis- tered some wholesome correction to the prisoner.—Mr ralbotinformed the Bench that the officer lost his temper with the man and strut* him when in Sankey-erreet.— Thomas Hough corroborated.—The Chief Constable said the prisoner had been before the Court 14 ~imes pre- viously and had blen imprisoned for assaulting the police.—The Bench committed Hai to gaol for three months with hard labour. The Chairman thanked Hough for the assistance he rendered to the Constable and said he would receive the usual reward, The Thrich were much obliged to hiim and to anyone who came to the relief of the police who vere very often at the mercy of a lot of ruffians and received very Dad treatment.—The Chief Constable said the case was another argument in favour of having a lock-up at Sankey Bridges in ad lition to the police station. 'rhe officer had to strugee with the prisoner for over a mile.

Stevenson-street, was summune.t for assaulting Hannah Steviason. 16, Stevenson-street.—Complainant,who appeared in the witness box with a badly discoloured face, gave evidence to the effect that there had been a neighbours' quarrel at the back of her house and she was standing at the back yard door.—Defend- and came up to her and made use of a foul expression. She was so indignant at this that she struck the man a blow on the side of the face. Defendant there- upon thrashed her severely, and butted her in the breast with his head. she wee blvk ant blue all over her body. Dtfendaut '• gave her a lot more than she seat."—For the oefeace witnesses were c riled and stated that Mrs Stevenson was using filthy language. She stripped her sleeves up and hit Richards. aid he put up his hand in self defence. He did not touch the complainant with his head and did riot strike her wilfully. During the hearing of the case complainant became very exc ted and ultimately went into hysterics, having to be carried out of court —The chairman said the defendant would be fined 5s and ts.—Mr Thornton: The decision is certainly not unanimous. Hanover-street. the horse foreman. was summoned for causing it to be wotked.—lnspeotor Print. R.S.P.O a. said he Was on duty in Queen-street and taw Fitzpatrick driving a 'bus to which were attached three horses. Noticing the middle one was lame he stopped it and made an examination. He found an old suppovating sore abodt the size of a five shill- ing piece At the top of the to lar and there were also wounds on the near and off side of the animal, one being the size of a two shilling niece It was suffering from lameness caused by sprained tendons. CoNSTIBL7 VIOLENTLY ASSAULTED—A PRISONER'S ALLE- GATIoN.—WiIitam Ward, 5 Bakehouse-yard. was charged , with having been, drunk and disorderly in Bakehonse-yarcl on Saturday night and also with having assaulted P Phillips —.the constable stated that he was on duty at Bridge Foot about half past eight on Saturday night and re- ceived a cmnplaint that someone was fighting in Bakehouse- yard. He proceeded there and. found the prisoner who was drunk behaving in a very disorderly manner. He pat him Into the house but he came out again and challenged witness to fight. He took him into custody and he became very violent, kicking witness on the legs several times. Witness lead to obtain assistance to take him to the Police Statioa. John Wolfenden, pork butcher, said he was passiag B icehouse-yard and heard the constable shout for assistance. He went into the yard and saw prisoner who was very drunk kick the constable and pull him atow the yard. Witness assisted in taking the prisoner to the Police Station. Prisoner said the officer was drunk and mad.—The Chief Constable informed the magistrates that the officer was a total abstainer and Was one of the steadiest men in the force.—Sucerintendent alooagban said he wee at the Police Station when the prisoner was bmught in. He was drunk and v-ry violent —Prisoner said he was in his house when the officer came in and strusk hirn.—Mr Birchall : Such a statement is absurd—Prisoner's wife said the officer did go into the house. He was raving mad. In answer to the Caief Constable she said she die not try to ' rescue her husband. e:he was not there the whole time.— The Chief Constable said the priermer had been before the Court eleven times, and had had two months' imprisonment before for assaulting Vap police.—Prisoner s The polteernan assaulted me then. I expect justice this time.—The chair- man s+id the prisoner's statements were the result of his imagination. He must have been in a fit of madness. He would have to go to gaol for two mcnths with hard labour. Mr Wolfenden was thanked by the magistrates for the avistance be rendered to the officer Tag GAMBLINeI NUIsiNCE—SMART PlNES—Thomas Leff, a middle aged man living at 23. Dallam-lane, was sum- mooed for playing " banker" in Buckley street on August Ilth.—P.C. Turner said the defendant was gambling in company with sevea or eight others. considerably younger than himself. When caught he refused to give the names of any of the other offenders.—The Bench imposed a fine of 20s and costs Wish the oetion of a month's imprisonment Frank Burgess. 71, Wellington-street, was summoned for playing a game Palled brag" on land between Sutton- street ad the Electric Light Works on August 18:h.—P.O. Dutton- street. were each fined lOs for gambling iu Dutton-street on the 18th inst. TRESPASSING ON THE RAILWAT—BoYS FlNED.—Waller Whittle. 38. Knutsford-road, an Charles Je1113.6. 321, Knutsfoid-road, b)ys, were sumsnonel f,r trespassing on the I London and No;th West.rn Railway at Latchford, on JuIV 30th.—Detective Howells stated that the boys in company 11 with four others were seen to get on the line at Latchford I and commence to throw stones at the telegraph Insulators. Several of the insulators were broken. Prwieedings were 'being taken again,t the defendants only. because they were the West b3ys. The Railway Company suffered a great deal o datrags from boys tresp..saing on the lines, especially at Latchford and he asked the magistrates to make an example of the defendants, which might at as a deterrent—air Fireball remarked that it was a wonder that more accidents did not occur, when there was so rumen trespassing—Defen- dants were each fined 2s 6d. WOMAN TFIR3WN Our or A TRAP —Teresa Crolla, 17. Fennel-street, was summoned or driving without a light at 9.25 p.m. on the 15th inst. in linutsford-road.—P.O. Clough said he was in Knutsford-road and waa informed that a woman has been thrown out of a trap higher up the road. He preceeded th -re and saw the defendant in charge of a pony and trap. She was under the influence of drink but was not drunk." There was no lamp tea the vehicle. It appeared that she hal been thrown out by driving into an iron bar whore the tram lines were being laid. He allowed her to proceed home. Further along the road she dr ,ve into !mother obstruction.—Defendant said that when she drove !rite the first obstruction the lamp, which was lighted, fell into the road. She was so confused that she went on with- out it.—She was fined Sc and costs.

man Shaw-Green, Dr Fox and BirchalC A S.Slo Cass: —William Hall, a sailor, who from the effects of hard drinking was scarcely able to stand in the dock, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Bold- streot on Monday night. Constaole Turner sairl he was called to a yard off Bold-street, and found the prisoner en the ground struggling most violently. Ile thought the man was in an epileptle flt, and 'Natter an unsuccessful attempt to bring him round took him to the Infirmary where the doctor said he hal been drinking heavily and treated him with the stomach pump. He refused to detain him as an in-patient, and witness took him to the police statton.—The Chief Con- stable said the man told Mtn that he was employed on a vessel and left her at Runcorn on Monday. He then had £2 15s and had been drinking spirits ever since.—The Chairman said he was not In alit condition to be released.—

div.head: WARRINGTON STREET FATALITY. A Little Girl Run Over in Laira Street.
div.p: WARRINGTON STREET FATALITY. A Little Girl Run Over in Laira Street.

A Man Who Didn't Know His Father-in-law. The rad death of a little girl named Gertrude Sutton, aged one year and eight months, and residing at 7, Laira-street, formed the subject ot an inquiry which was opened at the Warrington Police S:ation on Tues- day morning by Mr S Brignouse, county coroner. From the facts a the case repored to the polce it appears that on Saturday evening, the child was crossing L tira -.,treet end was knocked down by a horse and spring cart driven by a man named McGinnis, in the employ -f Messrs Eddowes and Com- pany, mineral water manufacturers, Scotlaud-road. One of the wheels of the vehicle passed over her neck. She was taken to the infirmary, and Dr Mort pre- counted life to be extinct. At the time of the accident the vehicle was proceeding at a alow pace —At the inquest Mr Forahaw represented Messrs Eddowes and Company, and Mr Crompton (Messrs Browne and Crompton) appeared on behalf of We relatives of the deceased. Fred Windle, 11, Laira-street,stated that he witnessed the accident. One of the wheels of the cart went over the child's neck. The mother of the deceased also saw the occurrence, and fainted. The driver of the cart was going at a " moderate trot." He saw the driver after- wards and he found that he was quite sober.

By Mr Crompton : Tnere was sumeone in the cart with the driver. At the time ot th, accident—at least as soon as he saw it—the cnid wi.s under the horse's head. She vas the only child he saw. Witness aid not see a girl with her. Tne sun W'lB glaring at the time, and beyond that there was nothing to obstruct the view of the street, so far as witness c uid see.

13y Mr Forshaw : Tao driver was actending to his work, and he pulled up as soon as he could. Witness was under the impressioa at first that th- wheel would have stopped when it got to the child's neck. The driver tinged up the mom-nt the accident occurred, and took the chfid to the Infirmary. Attention was called to the impending accident by the shouts of the pe)ple in the st,eet. The Coroner : If 'll3 one had shouted would the driver have gone on without any knowledge of the accident ? Witness : I think so. No one could have pulled up 1 in time to prevent the accident. Tne Coroner : That's rather a large order. Richard McCilicni4, the driver of toe cirt in question, said it contained mineral waters. He was sitting over the wheel on the off-eide. A "chat)" was with him. He did not know much about him. Pressed by the C -ironer, witoesi admitted that the " chip " was named "Green" He believed his full name was John Green, and that he lived in Liira-street. He did "lot see the ' deceased until she was under the horse—until he felt the bump. He was going at aboat the rate of five miles an hour. He was looking out—looking after his busi- ness. He had had considerable experience in driving horses. By Mr Crompton : Toe " chap " who waa with him was hie father-in-law. (Laughter.) Mr Compton: Why did you not say so before ? Have you any object in concealing his identity ? Wha , object had you in coming here and telling the Coroner that you did not know that man, and c ierecting your- self now, and saying he was y ear fattier-in-law ? Where does he live? Witness replied that he believed be lived in Laira- , street. _

Thu Coroner : This man has created a very bad impression on my mind. Toe wicness was further exaraited, a`ter which the Coroner said he thought it would he neoesBary to adjaura the inquiry. Without prejudicing the case he had a strong suspicion t -tat the witness and his father in.law were chatting an the time of the accident. an that they were not looking along the tstreet. He did not understand how the police cl,cl flat get nold 0? the information before now that there was some one in the cart with the driver.

Insnectar Rawbotham replied that he asked ths wit- ness whether th.,re was any one with him and he led him to understand that he was alone. The Coroner, coatinuing said it created a bad impres- sion when a man said he did not koow his own fatlitr- in-law. The truth alwaj. s went furthest. If there was no reason for telling a lie, why should the witness have told it ? The man's own employers must he aisqueted with him. The jury and himself w-,uld take the trouble to come to the Parade-room a2,ain so that the father-in- law might give his version of the affair. They had no right to close the inquiry until they had heard every- thing about the matter. _ . . .

Mr Crompton: It is a qaiet street and there is nnthia to prevent one's visiun. You can see anyone 100 yards ahead. 'the Cormer said he would have a ride in a cart along the street in question before the adjourned inquiry and " see what he cou!d 8.e."

A Firor : Then-, is n ithing whatever to prevent any- one seeing what is in frorf of him. At ig a clear etreet. The Lquiry was tliert adj 'tuned until Friday morning neat at ten o'clock.and it was arranged that the father- in-law and tin driver sh ,uld av,ornpany the Coroner in his tour of iospection.
A Walton Labourer's Death.—Fatal Result of a Fall.

Mr SBrighonae,CountY-6Oroner, conducted an in- quest at the Police Station on Tuesday, relative to the death of William thasworth (60), a labourer at Dallam Forge.wlio lived at 12,Taylor-street, Lower Walton, and died at the Infirmary at eight o'clock on Saturdal night. From the evidence it appeared that on tqe 17th lust deceased went, to the Walton 'signal lox between nine and ten o'clock at night to take a supper to one of the signalmen. On his return he complained of having fallen at Walton arches and hurt himself. Dr Curtis was called in, and he found that the man had sustained a fracture of the collar-bone and. injuries to the right lung. He attended him until the following Wednesday, but he did not seem much better and he was re- moved to the Infirmary. He seemed to be improv- ing until the 24c1, whsa On returning from one of the outbuildings he collapsel. in the doorway, and al haarnorrhage. GREAT SANKEY PARISH COUNCIL.

Mr G Thompson presided over a meeting of the Great Sankey rarish Council which was held in the Board Schools on Tuesday evening. ThPre were also present—Messrs T Halton, Fulton Smith, Kilshaw and J Smith (clerk).

div.head: WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB.
div.p: WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB.
Meeting of Members.
Subscriptions Increased.

Oa Tueiday evening a special meeting a the mem- bers of the Warrington Rugby Fo )tball Club was held in the Workmen's Club, Marke; Place, Councillor Tinnioo presiJing. Tuere was a very large attendance cf members.

At the outset, Mr. H. ASHTON, the hon. secretary, gave an xplanation of the objects of the meeting, which were to raise the sabscriptions and make some alteration in the rules. th.? questiod or the amount of subscrip• tions had been, be said, a matter of concern to the Committee for Some time. As they were aware, an intimation was conveyed to them at toe annual meeting that by the ruling of the Northern Union the minimum charge of admi3sim to Nortivern !League matcnes was to be 61. in the coming ' season. It was not fair that the public only should bear the additional expense of the season, and it was pro- posed therefore to increase the subscription for mem- bers. He had consulted various representatives of !Lancashire and Yorkshire clubs, and found that the !subscription of the Warrington membors was the lowest !of the lot. Oldham members paid 155 and 10; ; 125 61. 85 61, and 65 • Batley, 73 61, 104 61, and 21s; Swinton 6s, 10s, and 125 61; Salford, 7s 6d and 124 61 ; Broughton. Rangers, 7361 and 2.1 entrance fee ; Runcorn, 24 61 entrance fee and 5s ; Widnes,la 61 entrance fee and si. The matter had been carefully considered. They all knew that the club was about to eater upon some heavy expenses in the coming season and it was, he thought, advisable that there should be an expression of opinion about the sub. scription. He hoped they would give tne matter their attention and begged to propose that the annual sub scription for ordinary members be 75 61 with an ! entrance fee of 2361; and honoriry members 123 63 with an entrancl fee of 2s 61.
Mr. PEMBERTON (ion. treasurer) seconded. Mr. J. JEFFREY ! What will be the prices for the general public ? Mr. ASEITON : The committee have dezided to charge 6d and 9d.

Mr H. Witthar, T.P., asked why the coinmittee thought it advisable to raise the subscriptions. He should like to sea the minute ef the committee recording the passing of any soon resolution, and then they would eee whose proposal it was.. At the last general meeting there was a good balance sheet and the club was going on ve:y well. Why did they double the subscriptions when the cub was doing well, and was able to give ume members presents and reduca the subscriptions of others to nil ? _ _

Mr. E, SANDERS said he thought Mr Wright overlooked the fact that tho exrvioditure of the club would be largely increased in the coming season. Lie thought 7.a 61 was little enough. Mr S W JEFFREY : Ia Mr Wright's requost with re- gard to the minute to be acceded to ? Me ,thirms said it was hardly fair te mention native. The committee wero perfecly unanimous in bringing forward the proposal. Mr F TURNER took exception to Mr Wright's remarks with regard to free members. D:d he understand that , because he had been made a free member for past services he had no right to vote or speak? If so he would give in his free card at once. (Applause).

, . Mr T I.;AyrEs said he was not certain whether he was the proposer or seconder of the resolution at the con, mitti.e meeting. He had something to do with it and was not ashamed to admit it. (Hear, hear). With regard to free membership he had devoted 10 or 12 years to the service of the club and he had earned his fre3 membership. Playing football had cost him pounds when players were not paid. (Hear, bear). There was not a single man who had had a prrsent from the club or been made a free nraiber who had not worked very hard to get it. (Appla use). The CHAIRMAN supported th 3 election of free life nrimbers for services rendered and said it was the practice of most clubs. Mr S WRIGRT Said he was convinced there were other members of the club who had rendered equal services and were not life members. Moreover he could rind nothing about the matter in the rules. Mr S W JEFFREY said he regrettrd that this matter bad been introduced into the discussion. They wanted to cultivate the best feeling among the players and the action of the committee in the past had been calculated to do FO. Alluding to the subscription he said the jump from 4s to 73 6d seemed rather a large one and be wouid propose as an amendment that the ordinary members' subscription be 63 and the honorary members 15s each with an entrance fee of 23 61. Be did not think they could face the prospective expenditure Out increasing the membership fee. Mr t; t,IIITH asked for the number of hon. members. The CHAIRMAN there are 85. and 415 ordinary mem- bers. The subscription from the hon members is about ijof the total subscriptions received by the club. Mr T BARNES senior seconded the amendment and was preparing to discuss life-membership when be was ruled out of order.

- Mr CRITCHLEY also supported the amendment. He thought 6s was not a tall figure for the members to pay, and under presmt conditions 15s was a fair sum for the bon. members to pay. Several otber amendments were proposed but fell to the ground for want of a seconder. - .
Mr JEFFREY'S ammdment was put to the meeting and can ied almost .utmoimously.

A proposed alteration of rule 9, having regard to the committees power to deal with players leaving the field before the conclusion of a match, or any member guilty of ungentlemanly conduct, either at a meeting or during play, was deemed unnecessary, and was with- drawn. The committee's proposal that each member must produce his match card to secure free admission was carried, and the meeting addei a rule giving the committee authority to elect life members at their discretion. A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the meeting.

div.head: DANGEROUS BRIDGE.
div.p: A DANGEROUS BRIDGE.

The Clerk reported that he had written to the Clerk of the County Council with reference to the condition of Halton's Bridge. In the commanication he pointed nut that the bridge crossed the brook which was the baundary between Penkgth and Sankey and the read before reaching the bridge had is steep gradient and twisted to such a degree that it was impossible for drivers to see round the bend. The Parish Council felt it their duty to call the County Council's attention to the serious risk attaching to the present condition of things and trusted that the High- ways and Bridges Committee would proceed to carry out such alterations as would be necessary to remove or modify the dangerous character of the road. In reply to this letter the clerk to the Couuty Council had written stating that the matter would be laid before the neat meeting of the Main Roads and Bridges Committee. Mr Halton remarked that the matter had been dlr.. curoed from time to time by toe Warrington Rural Dis- trict Council and plans had been prepared. He Wit; of the opinion that the Main Boads Committee had the improvement in contemplation as soon as they could find a favourable opp,riunity for carrying it out. It was a most dangerous bridge. As the road was a main one the improvement would not effect the rates of the district he was pleased to Fay.
POSTAL FACILITIES.
SUNDAY DELIVERY AND DESPLTCH REQUIRED.

-- The following letter from the General Post Office London, was read by the Clerk.—" Sire—With refer- ence to the application recently made by the Sankey Parish Council for the institution of a Sunday delivery of letters to callers at the Great Sankey Post Office and of a despalch from Sankey on Sunday evenings lam directed by the Postmaster General to enclose for the Council's information a copy of the regulations govern- ing the establishment of Sunday posts in rural districts. From the inquiry which has been MRde It is found that the coat of affording the Surday dt livery asked for with despatch the same morning would be warranted,and on receipt of the necessary resolution and assurance from the Council the matter will be further considered. It is regretted, however, that the circums:ances would not Warrant the establishment of a despatch from Sankey on Sunday evenings —Your obedient serosnt,W ROCHE. To the Clerk of the Sankey Parish Council." On the motion of Mr Halton, seconded by Mr Fulton Smith, it was decided "to accept the Post Office regula- tions as furnished by them," giving the assurance that the Council represented the views of the inhabitants generally. LIGHTING OF THE DISTRICT.. ARE THERE SUFFICIENT LAMPS

The Chairm—sn brought forward the qaestion of the lighting of the district. He said he dia not consider the lights were good enough for the money paid, and he did not think they had a sufficient number of lamps. Re had been approached by a great many people, and in his opinion the lamps were of no use unless they had more. About a dcz more were requited and he suggested that the Council should meet on some d irk night and go round the township to decide where the additional lamps should be placed. The lamp at Penketh- ane end had been placed in another position and that rendered it of little use. . _

Mr Halton : If we got more lamps it would probably involve a special rate. The Clerk informed Mr Halton that it would not. The Chairman thought they ought to get the lamps at a cbeap3r rate and said the prices charged for Stockton Heath were lower than those charged for Sankey. Mr Halton : If we had a large number we should get them much cneaper.

Mr Kilshaw did not think any more lamps were needed in Liverpool-road. Other neighbourhoods re- quired them more. Mr Fulton Smith : If the lichting system is so bad is there not a danger of tha Council getting lost when they go round ?...(Laughter.).
, It was ulti:nately decided that the Council should meet to consider the matter a fortnight hence and after- wards make am inspection of the distric.. This was all the business.

div.head: DEATH OF MRS. F. SLATER.
div.p: DEATH OF MRS. F. SLATER.

We report with regret the death of Mrs F Slater,wife of the R.V. F Slater, who for 20 year; was Vicar cf St. James's Church, Latchford, which took place at the Vicarage of St. Chaere Over,at four o'clock on Saturday afternoon. The deceased lady, who was 51 years of age, had been in failing health since March lest, and later accompanied by her husband, she went to Italy in the hope that the change would be beneficial. D had not that Effect, however, and Mrs Slater returned to Over much worse than when she left it, finally suc- cumbing to a painful internal complaiet. She leaves a husband and five children with whem much sympathy is (xpressad in their sad bereavement. Mre Slater passed peacefully away in the preserce ef all the members of the family, except one—Mrs Hoc- deco—who is in South Africa. The sad intelligence was received with great regra. On Sunday the flag at St. Chad's floated hal-mast, and the bells rang a mufilea peal. In the course of his sermon in the evening the Rev. Busby made a sympathetic reference te the loss the parish had sustained through the death of Mrs Slater. The deceased lady's favourite hyrons and anthems were sung by the congregation, who were visibly moved, and Mr Finrey e organist), played the Dead March in " During thPir three years' sojourn amongst the parishioners at Over, Mrs Slater proved a useful coadjutor to her husband, are.i as a friend to the sick and poor she will indeed he greatly missed. In connection with the church she was ever an active worker. The beautification and decoration of the sacred edifice were her especial delight, and the loveliness of the church was due to her artistic taste. She also re-organised the young teen's &tie class and the Girls' Friendly Society,both of which are now in a fairly prosperous condition. Previous to her coming to Over she was with her husband allied with the Parish of S: James, Latchford, Warrington, and on their departure her lab nit amongst them was specially recognised by the members of the congrega- tion. The fueeral took place on Wednesday. There was a memorial service the same evening at St Chad's Church. REFERENCE BY THE REV. F. E. POWELL.

The Rev. F. E. Powell, preaching at St James' Church, Latcnford, on Suaday morning, said that death had been very busy in their midst recently, and they were very sorry to hear of the .clzcesse of the wife of eon who had been vicar there for about 20 years. Mr Powell referred to the remarkable interest which Mrs Slater invariably displayed in all affairs connected with the parish.

div.head: EXAMINER, FRIDAY,
div.p: THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY,
A FURIOUS DRIVING CASE Employer admits Liability before the Judge.

At the Warrington County Court, last Thursday before his Honour Judge Bowen Rowlands, an ace tion was brought on behalf of Elsie Robinson, an infauf, by her next friend Philip Robinson, 72, Oil-In-lane, against Joseph Birchall, confectioner, Bridge-street, in which £5O was claimed as dam- ages for personal iniurie.,alleged to have been sus- tained in consequence of the negligence of his ser- vant, on the 23rd of March last, through furiously driving a horse and van in Orford-lane. Mr Browne,solicicor,represent3d the plaintiff and Mr Steele, solicitor, the defendant. Mr Browne stated that the child was 2 years and 7 months old, and a daughter of Mr Philip Robin- son, of 72 Orford-lane. On March 23rd, Mr Robin- son took the child out between twelve and one o'clock. The child was about a yard away from the footpath, when a horse attached to a van, in charge of a youth employed by the defendant, came along at a furious pace on the wrong aide of the road, and knocked the child down. Either the horse or one of the van wheels inflicted a wound on the child's head. The wound was a serious one and the child had to be taken to the Infirmary, where it was at- tended for a week, during which time, the doctor would say, be never expected her to recover. At the end of the week the child was taken with measles, and as the infirmary was not an infectious diseases hospital, notice had to be given to the par- ents to take the child out. The girl was then taken home and attended by Dr Curtis for something like three months. Subsequently it was found necessary to call in another medical gentleman, for the pur- pose of consultation. Dr Bowden, who was for 9 years a surgeon at the Warrington Infirmary, ' would state that he was called in, and that what- ever happened to the child, except for the promi- nent] scar on • the face, could not be attached to the accident. Tele evidence would be offered in fairness to the defendant. Three independent witnesses who happened to be in the street at the time would give evidence as to the accident. They were not related to either the plaintiff or defendant ; and, they would give 1 their evidence as they gave it at the Police Court. The defendant's servant was sum- moned at the Police Court for furious driving, and was defended by Mr Jenkins, who publicelly stated that he represented Mr Birchall. Taere were five magistrates on the Bench and after giving the case careful consideration they fined the defendant's servant 10s. Mr ,`.teel submitted this was not evidence.
Mr Browne replied that he would not have sub- mitted it to a jury; but be had no hesitation in tell- ing his Honour of the fact. His Honour It is quite right.. .

Mr Browne, continuing, said he wrote to the defendant on March 26th, calling his attention to the matter, and stating that unless he carried out his prmnise to see Mr Robinson, his instructions were to hold him liable for the damages and loss sustained ; and, if a reasonable offer was not made proceedings would be taken in due course. No reply was received to the letter. Time went on, and the shild continued to be unwell until the 24th of June. He then wrote again informing the defend- ant that proceedings would be taken unless reasonable terms were offered. No reply was re- ceived and they now came to the court, and found a highly technical defence set up, the defendant having paid money into court with a denial o! lia- bility. If Mr Birchall had only approached them ,in a reasonable manner before the action was brought, they would have met him. He had cora- pellel them to bring the matter into court, and five days before the time Mr Bircball paid £lO into court. The only common sense conclusion he could arrive at in this action was that Mr Birchall appeared to have said to himself : "I think I am liable, and I will chance it and pal £lO into court." It the defendant would now make a reasonable offer, they were willing, in order to save everybods 'll time to consider it. The only witness for the de- fence, at the Police Court proceedings was someone who had since departed for America, and they the plaintiffs) had a witness present who if called would controvert that evidence.

_ After a consultation betwPen Mr Steel and his client, and Mr Browne and Mr Steel, Mr Browne announced that be was glad to say His Honour's time would be saved. They would not take a judgment so as to save the hearing fee, and ask to withdraw the case. The terms wPre that the plaintiff should receive £lO alreacly paid into Court, with an additional £lO, and his (Mr Browne's) and witnesses' costs. _ .

Mr Steel, on behalf of Mr Birchen, said his in- structions were to the effect that at the time the letters were written, another solicitor was in the case, and was instructed to answer them. He now stated he received no such instrnctions. There was evidently some misunderstanding between Mr Birchen and his solicitor, which led to the letters remaining unanswered. Mr Birchen had gone to see Mr Robinson on one occasion, but be was nc.t in. He, however, saw Mr Robinson's sister, but she treated him jug rude manner, and be determined not tC) go there again. Mr Browne, interposing, said it was not so. Mr steel, proceeding, stated Mr Birchen also went to the Infirmary and made every inquiry about the child, and asked whether he weuld be allowed to send in luxuries and lays for her. He was told it. was against the regulations. He was sure his cheat had done everything possible under the cir- cumstances.

His Honour thought Mr Birchall had acted in a very proper manner, and had had no intention of being discourteous with regard to the letters. Such misunderstandings, however, always had a very bad effect upon juries,and as a rule people would he wise to answer lettsrs even if they denied liability. The settlement arrived at was a reasonable one for hoth sides. Defendants in these cases were some- times to be pitied because they were made lrable for the articns of others over whom they had no control at the time The case would be allowed to be withdrawn.

MEETING OF TUE PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE. A ni.eting of the S.ockton H ,ath Parochial Committee was held ia the National Schoo's, Stockton Heath, la:4 Thursday evenusg. There were present Messrs Clarke, Pearson, Mason. Pemberton, Mclntyre, Whitley with Geo F Ashton (clerk), ami J Farriovon (inspector). THE LIGE' lING OF THE TOWNSUIP.

The Clerk read the tollowing letter from tho Warrington Cuporation under date August 6:11.—" In reference to tour order of February 13th for new lamps at Stockton Heath no proper agriernent has deen entered into for incandevent burners in iiu of ordinary burners. We recommend a number 4 Kern burner similar to Weil in use on Wilderspool Causeway• We would undertake to fix. light, clean ancrinaintain a three-IgEt cluster at £5 10s per annum; a two light at £3 las 61 and a simile tight at £2 7a 6d. Ry converting the pres,nt gas borner of Victoria Square into a three light c uster ; Ellesmere-road and Victoria-road into a single cluster ; and Whitefield.road green. A two light cluster, it wouM cost about 20a per annum more: We could ;upply a number three Kern burner which would give one fourth less light at a reduced price or 4s 63 per burner per annum. If you would like to fix a r umber three Kern on trial Vie could do AO with the objnt of ccnvert- ir,g, all your ordinary lamps into incandescente. We do not recommend the ordinary C hurter as it gives less light per cubic feet of gas consumed. Unless we hear tc, the contrary the work will be in hand with- out delay so as to commence the half-year's ilighting on the ldt'h last." _

Toe Cl, rk informed the committee that he had asked the Corporation to cirro out the instructions given by the committee accordinz to his letter of the 13th February. They did not appear to have put in the liana odescents yet. Mr Mason said they had done so in the square andl in Whitefield-road—a two light cluster. At the corner of Ellesmere-road and Fairft=le-uad singlo iights bad not yet re.no provided. Mr Whitley said they hd not the pillars suitable for the incandescent light. Ile proposed that the lamp at the bottom of Chapel-lane should have an incandescent light. This was not seconded,

Mr Mason then proposed that an incandescent light with number 3 Kern burner at £2 33 be placed at ihe bottom of Chave!-lano and gimilar limhts be provided at the cortiPr of Ellrsmere-road and Fait firld road.
This was agreed to

Mr Pearson moved that the ruling of the Local government Board be obtained upon the question whether the committee had n"wer to c3mpal builders to take their drai as along a back passage insteaa of down the bark yard se at present. Mr Miarn etated that the Clerk ha l alr4adv given an opinion that the c)comittee hail not the power. Trv.C(Prk said ha would be pleaeed to have the ruling of the Local Linvernment Board, as the matter would then be settled once for all. Mr Mason seconded and the prcposition was agreed to. This was all the busincss of public intercst.

div.head: WAR.
div.p: THE WAR.
LATEST TELEGRAMS. --- Three Wounded Australians
Shot Down.
Stern Measures by the Government.

The War Office has issued the following despatch a from Lord Kitchener : Pretoria, August 25.—Sworn evidence has been brought to my notice by General Elliott that on June 6:n Lieutenant Malt, of the New South Wales Artillery, and Privates Harvey and Blunt veers allot down at Graspan, near Reitz.af ter they had surrendered. I have for warded to Steyn and Botha copies of these statements.
In view of the above despatch the following tele- gram has been sent by the Secretary of State for War to Lord Kktchener
" WAII OFFICE, AU,Sprit 23.

"We uaderstand you have as yet receieved no satisfactory assurances respecting the murder of our wounded at Vtakfontein. In view of the occurrences in your telegram of the 25th inst, we are of opinion that you should notify by proclama- tion that the members of any corn mando,by which such an outrage may be committed, who may be captured, and after trial proved to have been present on such an occasion, will be held guilty, whether they actually committed the deed or not ; that the leader of the commando will bc sentenced to death, and other members of the commando Punished by death or less sentence, according to the degree of their complicity."

div.head: HORTICULTURAL SHOW AT NEWTON.
div.p: HORTICULTURAL SHOW AT NEWTON.

Favoured with beautiful weather, the sixteenth annual exhibition in connection with the N wcon.le- Willows, Earlestown and District Horticultural Society passed off succeislully in a fi.ld placed at the disposal of the promoters by Mr John Randall on S attarday. In point of entries the show was a distinct improvement on previous Veers, the number of entries this year b sing 400, 150 in excess of last year. Toe exhibits were effectively etaged in a large marquee, and the gentlemen who officiated as judges were Messrs J Heaton,Aigburth J W Haresign, Kenyon Hall ; and J Clarke., Lymm. Of coarse the recent drought had affected the quality of many of the exhibits, but in spite of that they were superior to last year's mho w and they p ointed to the fact that there was increased skill in cultivation by tho exhibitors. The groups of plants formed an especially attractive display. The Haydack Brass Band efficie otly played selections of music during the aftern-mn and evening. It is intnresting to note that the Society is in a sound financial position. It commenced the year with a balarre in hani of £1 131 6.1 and th various items of rev snu s brou zht the receipts uo 'n £63 63 Oil.
