div.head: INNELLAN.
div.p: INNELLAN.
A Scottish Holiday Jaunt.

In all probability more people have visited Scot- land this year than in any previous twelve months and the reason for this is not far to seek. When there is an opportunity of killing two birds .with one stone it is usually taken, and in this simple fact lies the explanation of 93 many more. people than usual' ganging awe" to Scotland this parti- cular year. The way it appeals to the majority is this. Scotland is an unsurpassable place for holi- day-making and moreover the great Exhibition is in Glasgow, fio that by pitching upon the 'land o'cakes" for the summer holidays the tourist not only ensures himself an exceedin7 pleasant time that way but he also makes the visiting of the Exhibition a matter co simple of ex- ecution that it would be next door to sin not to seize the opportunity. I myself have been to Scotland this season and spent the first fortright of the current month among the hills, dales and lochs across the border. I have also visited the Exhibi- tion, but the chance of doing so was really a minor consideration, in fact the wettest of wet days, when nothing elqi could be done, was chossn for the puip6se, and quite .sufficient it proved. There is a deadly sameness—l nearly said dullness—about exhibitions and there is nothing sufficiently re- mark able about the one at Glasgow to account for the tremendous fuss made on its account. It is big, and in many respects imposing, but it is after all meroly an exhibition of things, only a small per- centage of which the average individual is really interested in. But as a method of tiring one out, in double quick time it would teke a lot of beating. A whole day climbing mountains takes nothing like so much out of one physically as does a day's prowling round an exhibition. However, the Glasgow people are very proud of their Exhibition, and as it is undoubtedly one of the best of its kind, they are entitled to be so. But, personally, I am glad we took a wet day when we " did" the Exhibition. Having finished off the Exhibition I can now turn to the holiday proper and its many delights. We were a party of eleven, and our camping groune was Innellan, one of the prettiest and quietest pieces on the Firth of Clyde, with Rothesay only half a dozen miles to the south, and Dunoon a shorter distance to the north. It is somewhat necessary for me to give you Innellante nearest neighbours in order that you may accurately locate the place. Tnere are different ways of getting there, but in the opinion of at least four of us, per steamer from Lice-pool is far the best. We tried it and we reckon to know. The others went by train as far as Greenock, where we arrived the same morning by boat. Of course we did not all start at the same time. We four who braved the terrors of the ocean—conspicuous by their absence--left Liverpool at noon on Friday. August 2nd, and the remainder of the party not , until night. lo those who do not possess an inherent and unholy horror of the sea let me at once recommend the sail from Liverpool to Greenock. Better stop there, for the remainder of , the journey by water to Glasgow may undo all the good the previous portion has done. Like the Ship Canal, the Clyde talks, and up Glasgow way it talks very loud in the broadest Gaelic. It also bubbles, on warm days,' but that may be from exuberance of heppineee or, something else. You have heard of peeple bubbling, over with joy,of course. Well,that is exactly what the Clyde seems to be doing. Below Greenock,ho w- ever, it is entirely abevelreproach and at Innellan and the neighbouring places the water is clear as crystal. But to hark back to the voyage. It was a leisurely passage,occupying M hours, and land- ing us in Greenock at the convenient hour of 8 a.m During the whole of Friday, the 2nd. there was a fresh breeze blowing and when we had worked out of dock into the channel of the Mersey the odds seemed tube that the passage would be somewhat lively. This was not the case, it appeared later. The bre Z 3 was only sufficient to impart the slight- et motion to the boat and at the some time simply force the ozone into one's system, Everybody seemed to enjoy it and after having got one's bunk for the night seeured.the time was generally spent on deck. The Point of Ayre Was passed at dusk, and than the moon came out.bathing the glittering ocean in a silvery rad;ance that was indescribably lovely. Just before turning in we rounded the Mull of Galloway—or Gall of Mulloway as we disrespectfully dubbel it—passing quits close to the rngzed looking cliffs. Then oblivion for a few hours.and on decn again at daven,--a dull, Obiy dawn, with banks of cloud covering the crest of the Isle of Arran's lofty range of meuntains,which were clearly visible a few miles to our west. Due south Ailsa Craig was just discernible, and it was a source of some regret that we bad not the oppor- tunity of a closer view of thie famous rock. We steamed elowly up the Firth and as the day grew older the light improved and the clouds slid away towards the horizon. Goat Fell, Arran's highest peak, occasionally cleared and we called to mind the notorious Lawrie murder of a few years ago, when a London tourist was enticed to the summit of the mountain and there murdered for the gold be had upon him. It was a dark and, blood-thirsty deed, and Goat Fell looks a fitting place for such a crime, aheunding as it does in black, precipitous crags. To the east the Ayrshire coast was visible and as we proceeded the waters narrowed. The Cumbraes were passed and then the Isle of Bute. Next Clnie Inellan, which we were able to make out with the ail of the map, and then round Clech Point to Greenock. A vveie here of three-quarters of an hour and then on board the Columba, where we were joined by the rest. of the party, looking none the better for their night in the train. On the contrary we who had sailed were several shades browner and feeling immeasurably benefited by the bracing voyage. The Columba, a 24 knot paddle bee., made short work of the journey down to Innellan, where we landed about ten a.m, and made straight for the "diggings " we had previ- ously secured. It was a bright, breezy day and our holiday resort looked psrticularly charming with its background of well-wooded hill., and handsome villas peeping out from among the trees. Innellan is a fine centre for the, tourist. though there are probably placee even better situated. But you cannot grumble when fast steamers call every few minutes with the punctuality of trains and take you at a very cheap rate to some of the bonniest places in all " Bonnie Scotland." The Kylee of Blom was one of our earliest expeditions,the vessel first call- ing at Rothesay, the most popular of the Clyde watering places. To my mind there is too much of Deuelae. about Rethesay, though no fault can be found with the situation or scenic attractions of either place. Rethesay Bay is exceedingly charming, and the view across to Loch Striven and the lofty mountains beyond is one nut easily surpassed. The Kyles, or ] narrows of Bute, are not so narrow as a glance at the map leads one to think. They are nowhere less than a mile in width, but the sail through is an experience not to be forgotten. Owing to the circular nature of the tour the view is continually changing, loch opening out after loch, and moun- tain after mountain coming into view. Some of the small places situated along the Kyles, such as Coliatraive and Tighnahruaich, look like veritable little Paradises, so ideal are theiesituation ared surroundings. Another fine tour is the one which, after leaving the Kyles goes round Ardlamont Point, and thence up Loch Fyne to the Cerophell capital of Inveraray. Loch Fyne is famous equally for its kippers and for the fact that it is the largest of the arms of the Clyde. For fifty miles it penetrates inland, and the scenery right along is superb. In- veraray itself lies 40 miles from the mouth of the frech,and though a capital town is only a steal sleepy place.lignified by the fine caetie of the Earl of Argyll By the way, the steamer on which' we sailed to Invsreray had OR board a band of juvenile pipers who made a fine "skirl "every time the vessel approached the pier of one of the many ' calling places. Whether the idea was to charm the , hesitating teuriet on board or not we were unable to discover, but the pipers were only industrious ] , when we touched pore. Perhaps the finest excur- sion of the many we undertook was the one to the , nob Roy country by way of Loch Long, Arrochar, , and Tarbet. The twenty-two miles sail to Arrochar, , at the head of the loch, was as usual. a treat to the 1 ' lover of mountain scenery. At Arrochar woe leave , the steamer and walk a mile and a half along a , beautifully wooded lane to Tarbet on Loch ; Lomond. Here one of the lake steamers takes , you either up or down tha 35 miles of fresh , water as you may desire. There was a fine . crowd doing the round on the day we went, and the ancient dame 'who sines persistently" Bonnie Loch Lomond, on Tarbet pier seemed to do a good business in bawbees. We sailed up the loch to Inverenaid and had lunch at the foot of the fine falls here, and afterwards took one of the smart little steamers right down the loch to Balloch,pass-

rig close under the shoulder of lofty Ben Lomond en route. The whole country round about here reeks with romance and tales of slaughter. At Rowardennan, where the climbers of Ben Lomond usually leave the steamer, the loch is narrowest and deepest, and with Ben Lomond on the right and half a dozen other "big Bens: in close order the view up to the head of the loch is awesome enough. Just here too is a cavern among the rocks known as Rob Royes prison. It Yens here that Macgregor used to interview his captives. When they could not see their way to meet his views a dip in the waters of the loch sometimes hastened a change of mind. Other tones there are without number, including the Isle of Arran, the Cumbraes,Largs, Wemyss Bay (pronounced Weems) Ste. We did not attempt to do them all because, naturally enough I think, we wanted a little rest mingling with tee sightsee- ing, There is only one drawback"to Innellan and that is the paucity of walks in the neighbourhood, at any rate while the shooting season is on. The moors are all preserved and we were warned off twice before we reluctantly sub- mitted to the inevitable. Notices of the following sweet nature were frequently met!! with : " Tres- passers will be prosecuted. Dogs will be shot." Supposing the trespasser was mistaken for the dog? Fortunately we escaped a skin-full of pellets and so did the dog we hari with us. Still it was annoying to have one's rambles cut Po short. There was little choice between walking to Toward Point southward, or Dunoon, northward. To vary the proceedings we now and then went a-fishing in one of the small rowing boats, but we canolit nothing but three crabs in three excursion. Luck and the flail were against us. Still the rowing was very enjoyable, and the panorama from the middle of the eetuary exceedingly attractive, so thet we mild afford to be ,ephilosophical even if the fish weuld not remain long enouehon the hook to be haul- ed i 1. They took the bait readily enough, and some of them ought to be the bett-r for the attention we bestowed upon them in the shape of good fat mussele: Then there was cycling. Seven of its had our mitehines and we had Some enjoyable excursions and pirenies inland and up the locha. One ride in particular lam nit likely to forget in a burry. An inefficient map show ee lie an excel- lent round by way of Denoon, Holy Loch, Loch Bob, Strachurolown Loch Fyne to Otter Farry,and then aerose country to Innellan. Four-fifths of the journey were magnificent. The ride along Loch Eck is remarkably fine, and then down Loch Fyne from the pretty village of Strachur, it was ea milli, charming though not so wild. As far as Otter Ferry all was plain sailing, except that the read was generally rough and stony, but at OVer a thunder- etorni favoured us with a call. It rained as it only knows how to rain in the monntaine. hut 33 we were ensconced in the only Inn and having a rare good tea, we could afford to be, ence more, philo- sophic. In about an hour the rain ceased, and we set off across-country. It was more over than across! The road immediately gave us a taste of its quality by dwindling to a cart track and going straight up over a moor. It was unridable both owing to gradient and surface. After traversing a couple of miles we had got pretty well 110 in the world. Then the road forked and we took the half which looked the most promising. Another couple of miles steady plugging over the moor, mostly on foot, and the road finished up in a farm-vare.where ' we were immediately the objects of considerable I interest to the farm-folk who had apperently never seen a cyclist before. and certeinly not three of them in their own farmyard. There was no other building in sight and a scene more desolate could hardly have been imagined. Bleak moorland and bare hillside whichever way one looked ! Of course we had to retrace our footsteps to the fork in the track and take the remaining portion. This we did, and were just a little inclined to revile at fate when we found that nut path now went slap over the mountain top. Excelsior ! We plodded. on, pushing the " bikes " before us, and. going steadily up at an angle of about 1 in 12, with the rain carefully keeping our bearingefrom gettino too hot. Two miles of hard work at last landed us at the top, wet through, but still . capable of admiring the exteneive view we had in several directions. Time was flying, how- ever, and if we meant to be off the maintain before dark we had to keep moving, so for a short distance over the brow at the mountain we rode until the machines began to gain even on two rim-brakes, owing to the gradient and the water on the rims. The down aide ef the mountain proved to be steeper than the other, and it was not the easiest of taelesl holding the machines back down a slope sometimes equal to that on the roof of a hou.e. Spectacularly the tramp was very fine, though we found cause in numerous ravines to rejoice that the daylight lasted until we were once more on a cycling road. Before mounting, most of our Remit eole oil wee poured on the naked chains and then we set off once more, with about 24 miles before US, Rain had now ceased to fell, but the roads were covered with water. A few miles were reeled off in good time and just when darkness had closed in one of us had a puncture, The flinty road had gashed the tyre, and we ware well over half an hour in repairing the damage by the fickle light of a cycle-lamp. Even the puncture was viewed as quite one of the items on the programme, hut one thing—or rather a myriad of things—contrived at last to break through our fortitude. There were midges by the million,andlwhile we struggled with the punctured tube the little fiends bit and bit till our fluency of comment was quite exhausted. The heat of our rage was only equalled by the coldness of our feet, which were feeling decidedly uncom bitable owing to the wetting received. When we resumed it was found that only one lamp in the three would burn, and the cup of our misfortunes s oerned pretty full when the road rook us over another moor and Was unridahle for quite three milm, Cam more, "Ex- celsior" ! Alternately riding and walking we made moderate progress,nerrowly escaping a catastrophe on one occasion as our leader suddenly found his front wheel inches from a low stone wall which proved to be part of a bridge turning -et right angles to the road we bad followed. Below we could hear some mountain torrent roaring along in the styoian blackness of the nieht. An- other spell of solitude and hard work followed by very steep, stony descent to the shores of Lock Striven, which we struck near the hea.l. and Hurrah! there was the glimmering light of a cottage. Alas! it proved to be on the other side of the water, but our dieappointrnent had only jest begun to he keenly felt when we espied another beacen ahead. This time we were in luck and after rousing the simple country folk we succeeded in getting oil enough to add a e.cond light. The third was hopeless, the lamp being an acetylene with a leak below the burner, which even soap would not render gas-tight The "man &the hoise " told US we hid another three miles up-hill, and then it was nearly all down to Dunnon, which was about nine miles away. That three miles had mostly to be walked, but we A were warm and dry and cheerful again now, and made better progress. The drop to Daimon was long and eteady,and eventually we discovered it to be from Glenleen. With brakes almost constantly hard on, and the rough road jolting us from the saddle every now and then, we quite revelled in the stretch of free-wheeling. First, the lights of the yachts on Holy Loch came in view, and very anon We had left the mountains behind us and at 12 30 we were swimming through the wet tr.Ftts of Duncan. The'rernaining four miles to Innellan were done in good timemnd at last we were home, after one of the hardeet and longeet days the three of hot had ever experienced. With the exception of a fierce hunger we aged nothing, and that satiefied, together with a night's rest, WA were fit for anything the following morning. However , it took half the day to get the machines clean once I more and the chains and break-springs in prnoer working order. Most of our excursions awbeel after this were of a more mo seat nature, and did net include the conquest of moor- land and mountain. The weather was vari- able—in fact it rained every day of the fortnight —but We soon formed an intimate knowledge of Scotch mists, awl familiarity event- ually bred contempt. There was plenty of sunshine at times, and there were only twedere when it was too wet to get out, so things might have been worse. They might also have been better, but there is nothing like making the beet of matters, especially whenithey am so. unalm.rable as are the climatic conditione. The ph. iloso.phic temperament gets full scope. and the individual is none the worse for that. Certainly, we were n.o;so,apnh4,rB and all vir of us couldn't claim honestly to be phil were merely ordinary folk determined to enjoy ourselves and W 3 did. E V W.

THE EXAMINER FRIDAY, AUGUST 309 1901 BREWSTER SESSIONS. RUNCORN. Applications for New Licences Refused. The Runcorn Brewster Sessions were largely attended on Monday last, and the magistrates present were called upon to hear two applications—the evergreen Partington applicetion, and a new application by Mt Richard Abel, of eirofton Lodge, Runcorn. The Bench inoluded : Messrs A Thomas F J Norman, G L Davies,A. It Norman, 9 Taylor, J Pritclaard, E Imison, and R H Posnett, whilst amongst the general public we noticed : The Revs A Wells (superintendent Wesleyan circuit) ; B Foster (Camden), J Osborne (Coagregationalist), 9 Morris (Presbyterian), Mr H Baker, Mr W Handley Mr W Collier, and several members of the British Women's Temperance Association. THE POLICE REPORT. Superintendent George Ennien said he had the honour to submit his annual report with reference to the conduct of licensed victuallers and beer- sellers in the Runcorn Police Division for tea past year. There wess 44 licensed victuallers, 52 bestsellers, and five others with licences to sell off the premises, a total of 101 giving an average of 206 of the population to each licence. One licensed victualler was proceeded against dung the year but not convicted ; being a deer of one proceeded against and one convicted. Three beersellers had been proceeded against and convicted ; being an increase of one proceeded against and one convicted during the year. One hundred and seventy-five persons had been proceeded against for drunkenness, 165 of whom were convicted ; as compared with 201 persons proceeded against, and 192 convicted for the preceding year ; being a decrease of 25 persons proceeded against and convicted, as com- pared with the preceding year. A list was also submit- ted by the Sup-rintendent showing the name of the liceac-holeers who had been reported by the pollee for serving intoxicating liquor to chiidren apparently under the age of 13 lyears.—The average for the population was based on toe last census. Tee Ceairman said the report was a most satisfactory I one, and pointed out that the average of the population to each house was taken for the whole district, and not for the town of Runcorn alone. Hi noticed that one licensee was convicted en August 7th last year, but did not know bow it was included in the present list. Superintendent Ennioa explained that the annual report was made up to the end of July in each year,and net up to the date of the Brewster Sessions. The Chairman said it appeared they had had only one conviction, in which case they had not had the infertnetien up before them when the license was renewed last year: Superintendent Ennion agreed that such was the case. THE RENEWALS. Mr Johnson,the magistrates' clerk,then asked if there were any objections to any of the renewals being granted. Superintendent Ennion intimated the Police knew of none, and The Chairman announced the whole of them would be granted. THE ALTSIJN INN—.LAPSE OF THE LICENCE. Superintendent Eenion etated he bad also instructions from his Chief Constable to intimate that en the 23rd of July last sear James Wood, applied for temporary authority to sell at the 6' Melon Inn," Nelson-street, which had:been clessd fsr some time previously. Wood was advised to appear at the last annual Licensing Sessions (August 27th, 1900), but failed to do, so con- sequently the licence lapsed. A TRANSFER. The licence of the Queen's Hotel, Waterloo-road, was transferred from Mr Thomas Whitfield, to Mr. James Brooks, THE PARTINGTON APPLICATION, REFUSED AGAIN Me George Partington. grocer, Balfour-otreet,applied for on off-licence, to gal at a house in Balfour-street, the property of his wife. Mr Madden,barrister, Liverpool (instructed by Messrs Bremner Sons and Corlett, Liverpool), appeared in sup- port of the application ; and Mr E Davies, of Messrs. Lewis and Davies, solicitors, Liverpool opposed. Mr Madden in his opening stated the application was the eighth made by Mr Partington. It was for an ' off beer licence," from premises in Balfou: street, Runcorn. He did not think it would be conten dtbat the place was not fit for the granting of a licence of that charac- ter. Oa the occasion of the 3rd or 4th application it had been shown there were some 300 people in the im- mediate district, who were in favour of such a licence. In addition, too, there had been same five or six new houses built there in the last few years, and the popula- tion of the place showed a steady increase. The district was at present subjeot to the tyranny of "tied houses," and it was a shocking thing to think people eould not get beer where they liked. He pointed out the fact that the " off-licence " applied for would be an advantage to the neighbourhood without encouraging or necessitating any of the workperople's wives to go to the publie house, and as it was their in- tention to give up the grocery business altogether it would not be open to the construction that grocers licences generally were. The tied houses did not meet the needs of the district, and he hoped the Beach would decide, on seeing the greatneed of a free house for the district "that the time had come when an off bear licence should be granted." Mr George Partington. the applicant stated he was a grocer, carrying on business in Balfour-ecreet,Runcorn. Be proved the service of the necessary notices. It' wee his own application and he woe under agreement with no brewery company whatever. !The premises belonged to his wife and were valued at £22 lOnTtey were situate in the Heath Ward, in which ward there was only one other public house (" The Traveller's Rest") which being on the top of Runcorn Hill, he did net think WAS in a suitable place to meet the needs of the district. The next nearest public house was the "Lion,' but both were about lof a mile from his place. The next most convenient was the " Railway." None of the houses named were free. The district was principally a residential one and contained about 2.300 inhabitants; some owners of their own houses and even magistrates. As far as he remembered some 295 occupiers signed a petition in favour of his having a licence, on the occasion of the 3rd or 4th appli- cation. By her D evice. He had circularised the district, and the circular produced was his. He complained of unfair influences being used against him in the circular, but he did not attach them to Mr Davies or the magistrates. There were untrue statements made outside the Court. Mr Davies : Do you sugeeSt that the magistrates in Question acted upon anything but the evidenc3 adduced in court ?—Witness would not say that. Mr Davies : Do Tots think it is th right way to pro- ceed ? Don't you think it is a rather novel way ? Witness did notthink it wrong. Witness then admitted that on a previous occasion there was an agreement with his wife and the Brewery Company. But for all that he was not a trafficker in licences. Mr Davies : As a matter of fact wag there not an attempt to get the magistrates to traffic in licences ; and a pronesal to do away with some other licences for this one.—VVitnele pressed, admitted this. By Superintendent Eanion : flare were 3or 4 other grocers in the neighbourhood whom had opened since he first went there, arid the grocery business was not so profitable now. Mr Madden to the Saperintea lent : Are you opposing the licence ? Superintendent Ennion Yes, on behalf of the police. Peter Rudley , pump driver, residing in Lightburne Byrov-street ; George Stock, street ; John Atherton enginesee fitter, Wee'fi'l.road ; and John Baker,holler maker, of Askridge-streer, then testified to the teed of a licence such as applied for for the district. Samuel Gregory, Detective Sergeant of Ponce. Rini- corn, said he resided in Lightburn-=treet for 13 months, and knew the district well. It was his honest opinion that it would be an advantage to the district to have a freehou.e there. By Mr Davies : He was not there with his superior's knowledge ; and his superior had not had a proof of his testimony. Mr Davies did not think it was right for a police officer to be called on to give evidence in a case where his superior opposed. Mr Madden objscted to the way Mr Davit.; was ques- tioning the cfficer. It was a traversity at joetice, and- he was surprised at any advocate who objected to them nutting anybody they liked forward. The Chairman remarked that whatever Sergeant Gre- gory said in the ease would Rot:injure him in any way. Mr Madden then intimated that the case for the application wag closed. Mr Davies severely criticised what he called objection- able practices in an unique case. The applicant had shown an utter disregard to tile expression of the Bench last year when the caee was dismissed with the remark that they felled to see that any frr3h evidence had been adduced. Mr P atineton had not justified himself in the light of that expression. Touching on the questions of calling the police officer, he contended that it was all very well to cell anybody they liked if the applicant's character was in question, but to call a police officer to oppose a police force be characterisee as an unfair thing. The only new feature suggested was that a number of houses—fine or six— had been built, but were not occupied. They had the history of the whole thing. The first year was the granting of a wine and spirit off licence, with which the Bench were not called upon to deal. Next year there Was an application for an " off beer." The third year a Brewe y Company figured in the applicatine. The year following a six days' licence woeld suffice, and eventually they wanted to run the whole thing as an "off beer" and the grocery business was to be set aside. Mr James Johnson, ehipwright. B alfeur Street, a teetotaler, and the Rev J Osborne, the Mense,Norrnan- road, testified to there being no need for the additional licence in the neighbourhood. The Chairman (Mr F J Norcsan)on behalf of the Bench ,then announced it was their opinion there was no fresh
eyidenee,and they were again unanimous in their re• fugal a the application.
AN ROTEL NEEDED AT RUNCORN.

OF TELE TOWN. Mr Richard Abel. of Crofton Lodge, Higher Runcorn, made application for a full licence for Crofton Lodge, the property of his wife. Mr Pugh, barrister. Liverpool (instructed bv Mr Joseph Burton, solicitor, RuneJrn) appeared in suppor". whilst the objectors were again represented by Mr E Davies.

Mr Pugh characterised the application as one which would fill a real need. The'house Crofton Ledge (lately occupied by Mr Chadwick) was the property of Mrs Abel, and plans were submitted. The Chairman intimated that the whole of the mem- bers of the Bench were fully acquainted with the house. and there would be no need to go into the details. Mr Pugh, continuing, contended that his client was prepared to give an undertaking that the house weuld have no bar, or standing mina for drinking, and that it was his intention of runiing the same as a first-class hotel. He would call evidence to show the need of such a place for the many merchants who came to the port of Runcorn, from Manchester, Liver- pool and the Potteries ; and of the great need felt by captains of vessels for hotel accommodation whilst their vessels were lying at the docks being dig_ charged or otherwise attended to. During 1900 50 foreign going vessels ente-ed the Runedorn Docks. re'. senting a tondage of 131,982 or an average of 2,357 tons, and each vessel toak from a fortnight to nix weeks to clear. Some 86 foreign going vessels entered the Shit, Canal, and the reeking vessels figured about 1,131 at Runcorn and 337 A« Runcorn for a twelvemonth. HA quoted those figurest shsw the very large dilating population :hero was to be dealt with, and for whose 'benefit it was intended that the house should be leonducted.

Mr Richard Abel, of Crofton Lodge, then bore nut Mr Pugh's opening statement. He proposed to have no outside trade, and to run the place as a first claEi hotel, with refreshments and sleeping accommodation. By Mr Davies : He had nreviously held the licence of the " Dike of Wellington," Weill ngton-;treet, but had never had any exaerience in hotel management. Questioned as to the origin of the applieatloo spoliesnt said it or:ginatad as the result of a garden party giuen by his wife in aid of the Nurse fund. Anyhow, it, W" talked of then. He hid seen no brewer or brewers' travellers, and was running it on his own. r Henry Lovatt, general ship sore dealer, Liverpool, spoke to the need of accommodation of a first-elm? character required in Runcorn. At present they bad to go to Liverpool for it: David Henry Dunning, on behalf of the Andertno Company; Davidson. a commercial traveller, for Messrs C H Elliott & Co, Birmingham ; William Chadwick. Commission agent; and William John Cole, marine wile- neer, also testified to the need they nerindlcallv felt of "an hotel." Their experience of hotel accomModation in Runcorn was not a vned one.
Frederick Whalley, 12, Norman-road, proved service of the usual notices.

r Mr Davies, on behalf of a number of property owners, raised serious objection to the granting of a lic.^.A. One fsctor was the isolation of the place and its diffi- culties for nonce enpervision. non with regard to the undertaking, Mr Abel was getting on in years, and though nassibly the undertaking would be carried out by himself, whilst the Magisterial Bench were there to see they were carried out AA Mr Pughtindicated, when it came to the question of suc- eessors it would be bard to ma v what would happen. Then with regard to the bar. It was said at first thee was to be no bar, then later an Mr Pugh spoke of a " service btr." This would open on a room each nide and the entrance hall In front, and there they bad the whole thing,
Mr Pugh : There will bo no bar; it will simply be a soi vice bar.

Mr Dtvies : ft is inmaterial what the adj ,ctive is, it does not enter into the composition of the noun. (TJeer. hear from the bola, of the Court). Continuing, Mr Davies p)inted out that if the need of an hotel was felt so greatly in the town it would be far the wiser course for the Bench to call upon the 44 licenael vintuallers, and 54 beersollers to perform that for which thPv were per/lardy licensed. At the conclusion of Mr Da.vies, address the Bench retired for a few minutes, and on retrrning into court
Thq Chairman said : We are nails unanimous in the refusal of the application,

div.p: DARESBURY DIVISION.

There OM very little business of public interest at the annual Hennaing sessions for the Dareshury division which were held at the Coort Hovise, Daresbory .on Tuesday morning. The magistrates on the Bench were Messrs 3:Charlton Parr (in the chair),W Long,J;Tinsley, H Nield and II Talbot.

div.head: BRAVERY REWARDED.
div.p: BRAVERY REWARDED.

Interesting Presentation to a N& Constable. " Only did a Policeman's Duty." There was a pleasing ceremouy at the 2 Police Court on Thursday morning whect prior commencement of the ordinary business of the Police Constable Clarke was presented by the ch; (Ildr T J Gillespie) with a medal and diploma al by the Rays! Humane Society, in recognition bravery in res-ming a boy from drowning on Jui Ile Chairman said that before the comment of the business he had been regnested to perfot most pleaaing duty of nresenting a medal and dii of the Royal Humane 9)ciety to Police Constable I

as a reward for his bravery in rescuing a la, drowning under very dane,erous circumstance Gillespie proceeded to read the particulars of the, supplied by the Chief Constable. It appeire( en Saturday, June B,:h as 4 15 p.m., James L berrow 13 years of are, was bathing with other s,, aldisused clay pit on Newton Common. He sank ibue ten yards from the side and as he did not rise, a shout arose that he sees drowned. P.C. Clerk() who W 34 between 200 and 300 yards distant was told and ran t° the spot, threw his helmet off and with his uniform 00 entered the pit which is shallow at the sides, gradeallf deepening to Bor 10 feet in the centre. The constable ilwarn a few yards and went overhead. A gire,!:e Noah Boswell, threw a rope which PC. Clarke grasped, found the boy with his leer., raise. him, and the °lnstable and the boy were pulled to the bank by Boswell. P.C. Clarke used Dr. Sylvesteee method of artificial respiration for 15 minutes, restoring animation, after which the boy was removed horn • Had it not been for the assistance rendered by Boswell. the officer might have lest his life, owing to being en- cumbered with the boy end mud. P.C. Clarke, it Ws3 stated,has served over 13 years in the force, had nothing but good recorded, and weare the merit badge, granted for good service when beset by a faros and overwhelm- ing mob Re also holds the St John ambulance certificate and applied that knowledee to reetote the boy. Co Unclog Mr Gillespie addressing P.C. Clarke said tt I ean only say I feel proud of you as an Englishman for lb° way in which you have done your duty. I am evi!" sure the gallant de-d you have done must be a great gratincetioa to yourself and I can only tell yo'i it is with feelings of very great pride that we recogniz3 /leering such a inemher of the force:' (Applause). Mr Gilleepie then handed the meal and diploma to P.C. Clarke and wished him good health and heppinese He should also like to Trier tion how very much indeetP they 'felt te Boswell for the assistance he rendered• was most gratifying when they found the outside pubel acting in such accord with the police. In receiving the awards P.C. Clarke said I WI very highly honoured in receiving the. medal and than ru very much for the kind remarks y,ir have made, r only did a policeman's duty and I feel that any ether constable wou d have done tie 831113 had he been in al place." (Applause.) Superintendent Higginbettern mentioned Oat Boswell had been rewarded by tie Chief Constable.

An album containing letters written by all the United States Presidents from Washington to Mainley was lately sold in Now Orleans for 1,000 dollars. A double drowning accident occured at Greenock on Tuesday night. A boy named Dunlop, aged nine, was engaged in fishing of a pier at the east end of the town. when be overbalanced himself and fell into the water. William Groves, a bystander, jumped in after him, but both were carried away by the tide and drowned.
